title: iPhone Duo's A20 Pro Chip Benchmarked Ahead of Launch
content:
The iPhone Duo unsurprisingly offers performance similar to the iPhone 18 Pro, according to an early iPhone Duo benchmark shared on Geekbench 7. Both devices are equipped with Apple's 2nm A20 Pro chip with a 6-core CPU and a 7-core GPU.


The benchmarked ‌iPhone Duo‌ (iPhone19,4) is running iOS 27.1, as expected, and it had a single-core score of 3986 and a multi-core score of 11067. That's in line with multiple benchmarks collected from ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max models.

Scores vary from test to test, so while the result does fall short of the top ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ benchmark scores, we're only viewing a single score. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has the same 6-core CPU with a 4.93GHz base frequency that's identified in ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ benchmarks, and it lists 11.30GB memory, which means 12GB of RAM.

While the ‌iPhone Duo‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models use the same A20 Pro chip, there could be differences in real-world performance based on thermal management, the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s two screens vs. a single screen, and other factors.

Apple says the A20 Pro offers up to 20 percent faster CPU performance than the A19 Pro and up to 40 percent faster GPU performance. GPU speeds were not tested.

title: 10 HomeView Features You Might Have Missed
content:
Apple plans to launch the HomeView on November 13, so we have a month to go until we can learn more about it. Right now, we're limited to the information Apple has shared and what members of the media learned during limited hands-on time.


We've rounded up some interesting HomeView tidbits you might have missed.

 	
Recipe walkthroughs - HomeView makes Safari recipes easier to follow by pulling out the ingredients and steps. You can tap on a "Start Cooking" button to get step-by-step instructions you can use as you cook. The device also supports multiple voice-activated timers.

 	
Siri access - You can say Siri (English only) or Hey ‌Siri‌ for hands-free access, but there are also options for activating ‌Siri‌ with a swipe down from the top of the display or using Type to ‌Siri‌.

 	
Apple Intelligence - HomeView has some Apple Intelligence features built in. You or members of your household can use ‌Siri‌ AI for general knowledge questions if you don't have an ‌Apple Intelligence‌ iPhone or iPad, but you do need one for any requests involving personal context.

 	
Guests - Personal data is private, but guests can control smart home accessories, check the weather, set timers, and play music. Visitors can also AirPlay audio to the HomeView using peer-to-peer discovery.

 	
Adaptable interface - HomeView can tell when someone is approaching and parts of the interface will change based on proximity. If someone is across the room, it shows less information in a larger view. As the person approaches, the view can change to show more information.

 	
Faces - HomeView has multiple customizable faces similar to watch faces. Apple says some faces can "wake with you in the morning, wind down with you at night." The Snoopy face, for example, has different animations based on time of day, weather, and holidays.

 	
Third-party apps - There's no App Store, but the HomeView has CarPlay-like software capabilities. It can show CarPlay audio and video apps from a linked iPhone. There are no ‌CarPlay‌ video apps except for Apple TV, so app developers will need to add support.

 	
Handoff - You can transfer songs, podcasts, calls, videos, and recipes from the iPhone to the HomeView.

 	
Live Activities - HomeView supports Live Activities, so if you have a timer running or get an incoming Intercom message, content will be visible while you use other apps.

 	
Sensors and HomeKit - The HomeView has temperature and humidity sensors that can be used in Home app scenes and automations. It also serves as a home hub for controlling HomeKit and Matter devices when you're away from home.

title: Which Apple Home Devices Get Siri AI, and When
content:
There's been some confusion about which of Apple's new and existing home devices will support Siri AI and when, because ‌Siri‌ AI isn't going to be available at launch on some products.


Devices With Siri AI


HomeView - Available at launch (November 13)

 	
Apple TV 4K (4th generation) - Available at launch (November 13)

 	
Apple TV 4K (3rd generation) - Available in tvOS 27.2

 	
Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) - Available in tvOS 27.2

 	
HomePod mini 2 - Ships October 30, ‌Siri‌ AI coming in a future software update


CNET suggesting the first HomePod mini would support Siri AI, Apple has since confirmed that's not the case.
No Siri AI Support


Original HomePod mini

 	
Original HomePod

 	
Original Apple TV 4K (no tvOS 27)

 	
Apple TV HD (no tvOS 27)


Unconfirmed


HomePod 2 - Possibly coming, with mentions in website metadata


Siri AI Requirements

On the ‌HomePod‌ and Apple TV 4K models that support ‌Siri‌ AI, the home owner in the Home app must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad on the latest version of the software. ‌Siri‌ AI has to be turned on, and it has to be set to a supported language. Other members of the household don't need an Apple Intelligence-enabled device once ‌Siri‌ AI is turned on, except for personal requests.

HomeView does not require an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or ‌iPad‌ for ‌Siri‌ AI, except for requests that use personal context.

HomePod mini 2 is English only and is limited to the United States, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the UK at launch.
EU Restrictions

‌Siri‌ AI is not available in the EU on the iPhone and ‌iPad‌, so ‌Siri‌ AI won't be available for home devices that support it. HomeView isn't even launching in the EU.
Siri AI Beta

Apple is still calling ‌Siri‌ AI a beta, and it will be in beta when it's available on HomeView, ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, and ‌HomePod mini 2‌.

content:
Apple plans to bring Apple Intelligence to China in iOS 27.3 after two years of regulatory delays, reports Bloomberg. Image Playground and the newer version of Genmoji will be missing, plus text generation tools will be limited.


The South China Morning Post today reported that China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology recently gave Apple network access permits to add Alibaba's Qwen and Tongyi Wanxiang models to the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and earlier iPhones, paving the way for an ‌Apple Intelligence‌ debut.

received initial clearance to launch ‌Apple Intelligence‌ in China in July, but needed additional clearance for a consumer launch.

China restricts foreign AI technology, which meant Apple had to partner with Alibaba and Baidu to launch ‌Apple Intelligence‌ in the country. Apple also has to allow the Chinese government to approve ongoing updates to the AI models.

Competing smartphone makers in China like Huawei have long offered artificial intelligence features, and Apple has been at a disadvantage without comparable tools.

title: OpenAI Says Ex-Employee Showed Its Device Plans to Apple
content:
OpenAI today suggested Apple could be using its trade secrets, the very thing Apple is already suing OpenAI for. In a court filing, OpenAI accused an ex-employee of giving sensitive data about an unreleased product to Apple.


The unnamed employee joined OpenAI from Apple and then returned after six months. OpenAI claims the person sent "over a hundred highly confidential files" to personal accounts, including manufacturing data and detailed images of at least one unreleased product. The former employee allegedly "made a presentation" on OpenAI product plans for Apple's senior leadership "months ago," and OpenAI is worried Apple could use that information to further its work on AI devices.
OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work. OpenAI has raised these issues directly with Apple, but to date, Apple has not provided OpenAI with the requested assurances that Apple is not in possession of, and has not used, OpenAI's trade secret and confidential information.

OpenAI asked the court for permission to investigate and pursue counterclaims if necessary. Apple told Reuters it has found no evidence to support OpenAI's claims and it has policies in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers.

Apple sued OpenAI in July. Apple says OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan stole trade secrets from Apple to develop new AI hardware. OpenAI called the lawsuit "careless, aggressive and oddly personal," stating that it does not "have, nor want, any of their trade secrets" because it is "much more interested in building innovative products and technologies that push the frontier."

Yesterday, the court partially granted Apple's request for expedited discovery. OpenAI has up to two weeks to hand over forensic evidence as well as materials used when interviewing former Apple employees. Liu, Tan, and Alyssa Peng, Liu's former Apple colleague, will need to sit for depositions after Apple gets the requested information.

Bloomberg says an injunction would "mark a potential setback" for OpenAI's hardware development efforts.

title: New Echo III T5 gives new Macs three PCI-E slots across Thunderbolt 5
content:
Sonnet's updated Thunderbolt 5 expansion lineup gives Mac mini, Mac Studio, and MacBook Pro users a way to connect up to three full-size PCIe cards with the newly updated Echo III T5.

Sonnettech releases new products
The Echo III T5 family brings PCIe expansion to Macs that don't have internal card slots. Audio engineers, video editors, and other professionals can connect specialized hardware for recording, video capture, networking, and storage without replacing their computers.
The systems support up to three full-height, full-length single-width PCIe cards, or one double-width card alongside a single-width card. They're compatible with computers equipped with Thunderbolt 5, Thunderbolt 4, or USB4 ports, although available bandwidth depends on the connection.
Each system uses one x16 and two x8 PCIe 3.1 slots. The systems support compatible non-GPU cards and are qualified by Avid for use with up to three Pro Tools HDX cards.

title: HomePod mini 2 can double as speakers for your Mac, if you have the right one
content:
Macworld





If you bought a Mac within the past three years, Apple offers a new feature with the HomePod mini 2 that you can take advantage of: the ability to set up the speakers as the default audio output device. However, Apple says this works only on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E or later, which Apple began incorporating into Macs in 2023.
To be more specific, the HomePod mini 2 can be used as default Mac speakers with: 
M2/M2 Pro or later Mac mini
M2 Pro/M2 Max or later Mac MacBook Pro
M2 Max/M2 Ultra or later  Mac Studio
M2 Ultra Mac Pro
M3 or later iMac
M3 or later MacBook Air
A single HomePod mini 2 can connect to the Mac, or a pair can be connected for stereo output. The mini 2’s four speaker surround soud setup works only with the new 4th generation Apple TV 4K. Learn more about the HomePod mini 2.
The HomePod mini 2, as well as older mini models and the larger HomePod can also connect to the Mac (and iPhone, iPad, iPod touch, and Apple TV 4K) via AirPlay, but this type of connection can’t be set as default, so you need to reconnect anytime you restart the device or log out. There’s also a slight lag when syncing up the audio, so it’s not the most ideal setup.
Interestingly, a footnote on the HomePod mini 2 tech specs website says the following in regards to the new Mac connectivity:
7. Compatible with HomePod mini 2 and HomePod (2nd generation) with support on all Mac desktops and laptops with Wi-Fi 6E or later.
That indicates that this connection method also works with the HomePod (2nd generation) as well, which was released in 2023 and is equipped with Wi-Fi 802.11n, not Wi-Fi 6E. Also the HomePod product page does not offer any details on Mac connectivity. We’ve reached out to Apple for clarification and will update this article should we get a response.

title: Parallels Desktop 27 for Mac review: Still the best way to run Windows
content:
Macworld





At a Glance

Good performance on capable Apple silicon Macs
Version upgrades included during an active subscription
Cons
Most editions require an annual subscription
Windows licensing can add to the cost
Demanding workloads need plenty of memory and processor power
Limited suitability for modern Windows games
Our Verdict 
Parallels Desktop remains our leading choice for Mac users who need a full Windows environment for work or development. Its easy setup and close integration with macOS make it approachable, while its advanced controls cater to more demanding users. Version 27 expands graphics capabilities, but the cost of Parallels and any required Windows license can be hard to justify for occasional use. Gaming compatibility remains a reason to try before buying.

Who should buy Parallels Desktop for Mac: Mac users who depend on Windows business software and developers who need multiple operating systems.
Who should skip Parallels Desktop for Mac: Skip Parallels if you only need occasional Windows access, mainly play modern Windows games, or have a tight budget.
The Mac is no longer dismissed as an insignificant niche market that struggles to compete with Microsoft Windows. But, even so, there are still times when many Mac users need to run apps and software that are only available for Windows PCs. Perhaps your employer uses particular business software that’s only available for Windows, or you may need to use a website that relies on some Windows-only technologies. Many developers need to test their apps and services on both Macs and PCs and, of course, there are all those AAA games that only run on Windows as well.
It used to be easy to install Windows on Macs, thanks to Apple’s Boot Camp software and the fact that from 2006 to 2020 all Macs used the same Intel processors as Windows PCs. However, with the advent of M-series Macs, Boot Camp is no more, so if you want to run Windows on a Mac you need to consider one of the various virtualization options that we feature in our roundup of the Best Virtual Machine software for Mac.
The advent of Apple’s own chips, aka Apple silicon, also means that the standard version of Windows, designed for X86 processors, won’t run on Arm-based chips like Apple’s M-series. If you want to run Windows on an M-series Mac you need the Arm version of Windows. 
Our top solution for running Windows on a Mac is Parallels Desktop. Read on to find out why in our full review of Parallels Desktop for Mac. 
What is Parallels Desktop for Mac?
Parallels Desktop lets you run Windows in a virtual machine on your Mac. Instead of restarting to switch operating systems, you can use Windows and Mac apps side by side. It is particularly useful if your employer relies on Windows-only software, your course requires a particular application, or you develop and test software on more than one platform.
Windows is the main attraction, but you can also create Linux and macOS virtual machines. These provide separate environments for testing software without changing your Mac’s main operating system.
We tested the Pro edition of Parallels Desktop 27. The core Windows setup and Mac integration are also relevant to Standard users; the edition comparison below explains which users should consider paying more.
What’s new in Parallels Desktop 27? 

				
					

				
			

Foundry




Version 27 concentrates on technical improvements rather than a long list of new interface features. It supports macOS 27 Golden Gate and requires Apple silicon; Intel Mac owners need to remain on an earlier version, such as Parallels Desktop 26. 
The most significant graphics change is support for OpenGL 4.3, which matters for professional Windows software such as GIS, engineering, and design applications.
The new driver uses Apple’s Metal graphics technology. Parallels reports OpenGL gains of up to 2.6 times over the previous driver, but these are the company’s measurements, rather than results from our review tests.
Parallels says full hardware acceleration for the new OpenGL driver requires an M3 or newer chip and macOS Sequoia 15 or later.
Version 27 also exposes SME2 instructions to Windows and Linux VMs on M4 and newer Macs. The advertised sevenfold gain applies to matrix computations measured in an Ubuntu VM on an M4 Pro; neural-network inference improved by up to 1.75 times. 
Enterprise additions include more ways to report license-key versus single-sign-on activation, distribute approved VM images through corporate storage, and deploy preconfigured Windows environments.
Parallels Desktop: Recent updates at a glance


ReleaseTimingMain changes

Parallels Desktop 26Ahead of macOS 26 TahoeAdopted Apple’s version numbering; added Tahoe and Windows 11 25H2 compatibility, host-storage visibility in Windows, and expanded business management controls.
Parallels Desktop 20.2Between versions 20 and 26Introduced support for running Intel-based Windows virtual machines on Apple silicon Macs through emulation.
Parallels Desktop 20September 2024Added macOS Sequoia and Windows 11 24H2 support, Apple Intelligence Writing Tools in Windows apps, Apple ID sign-in for supported macOS VMs, and faster file sharing.
Parallels Desktop 19.3March 2024Fixed graphics issues affecting Windows games, including Dark Souls II and Genshin Impact.
Parallels Desktop 19.2Between versions 19 and 19.3Added faster VM cloning, improved account sign-in, and fixed stability problems with virtual machines stored on external drives.
Parallels Desktop 19August 2023Introduced a redesigned interface, OpenGL 4.1 graphics support, Touch ID sign-in for Windows, and updated printing support for macOS Sonoma.

 



Should existing users upgrade?
The graphics changes make version 27 most interesting to users of demanding professional software. If your current version already runs your everyday Windows apps well, the upgrade may make less difference to your work.
For subscribers, new versions are included during the subscription term, so there is no separate upgrade fee. Owners of a one-time Standard license should weigh the new features and operating-system compatibility against the upgrade cost. Intel Mac owners cannot move to version 27.
Setup and ease of use

				
					

				
			
Parallels Control Center

Foundry




One of Parallels’ strengths is its polished, Mac-like interface. Installation is much like installing any other Mac app, and the Control Center guides you through creating a virtual machine.
It can download and install the Arm version of Windows 11 needed for the usual Windows VM setup on Apple silicon. This removes the need to find an installation image and manually configure everything before you can start work.
You still need a suitable Windows license. Parallels is Microsoft-authorized to run Windows 11 Pro and Enterprise on Apple silicon, and the Parallels website says users can bring an existing Windows 11 key if it is eligible to activate their installation.
Once Windows is installed, you install applications much as you would on a PC, subject to Windows on Arm compatibility. Configuration profiles help you choose settings for tasks such as productivity, development, or design work. You can then adjust the memory and processor allocation if necessary.
The 14-day trial is useful here: test your essential applications and peripherals on your own Mac before committing to a purchase.
Installing Windows using Parallels Desktop

				
					

				
			

Foundry




Parallels Desktop makes installing Windows straightforward, with an assistant that downloads Windows 11 and creates a virtual machine for you. On an Apple silicon Mac, it installs Windows 11 on Arm. Here’s how to get started:
Download and install Parallels Desktop. Open the app and choose Install Windows when prompted.
If you already use Parallels, create a new virtual machine. Open Control Center, click +, then choose Get Windows 11 from Microsoft > Continue > Install Windows.
Follow the installation prompts. Parallels downloads Windows and handles the virtual machine setup.
Activate Windows. Open Settings > System > Activation within Windows. Use an eligible existing license or follow the Microsoft Store option to buy one. Windows isn’t included in the price of Parallels Desktop.
Install your Windows applications. Check that your essential software works before committing to a Parallels subscription.
You don’t need a special Arm license: Windows 11 Pro product keys work with both Intel and Arm versions. However, each Windows installation needs its own license, and an existing license must be eligible for reuse or transfer. Read our guide to How to use Parallels Desktop to run Windows on a Mac for more information. 
Performance and Windows app compatibility
Parallels is best judged by how well it runs the software you actually need. Everyday productivity applications are a less demanding proposition than large 3D projects or multiple development environments, and both Windows and macOS need a share of your Mac’s resources.
Parallels lists 8GB of Mac memory as the minimum for version 27 and recommends 16GB or more for best performance. It recommends M3 or newer graphics for demanding workloads.
A Mac with 8GB can meet the minimum without being an ideal choice for running Windows alongside memory-hungry Mac apps. The trial is particularly important if you are using a lower-specification Mac.
Windows on Arm can run many applications originally written for Intel PCs, but compatibility is not universal. The ability to install Windows does not guarantee that every application, plug-in, or peripheral will work correctly.
There are some limits relevant to developers noted by Parallels: nested virtualization, Hyper-V, and WSL2 are unavailable in its Windows environment on Apple silicon. It suggests WSL1 as an alternative.
Business users may wish to run Windows-only applications such as Access, Visio, Project, and Power BI, as well as Windows-specific Office add-ons. 
Can you play Windows games?

				
					

				
			A Windows game running alongside Safari.

Foundry




Gaming is more variable. Parallels Desktop supports DirectX 11.1, while many modern Windows games need DirectX 12. 
In our tests on an M4 Pro Mac mini, Skyrim ran without problems at a smoothly playable 50fps at 1920×1080 using its default graphics settings. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 suffered graphics glitches. 
If gaming is your main reason for buying, compare Parallels with a more games-focused option such as CrossOver and check support for the particular titles you want to play. Paying for Pro does not guarantee that an incompatible game will work. Read our roundup of the Best Games to play on Mac.
How well does Windows integrate with macOS?

				
					

				
			
Parallels Coherence mode with Edge and Safari
.
Foundry




Integration is where Parallels makes its strongest impression. A Windows VM can sit in its own window, expand to full screen, or use Coherence mode to hide the Windows desktop and leave individual Windows apps alongside your Mac apps.
You can switch between applications with Command-Tab and keep Windows applications in the Mac’s Dock. Coherence is especially useful if you need one Windows app while spending the rest of your day in macOS.
Copying and pasting between applications, dragging files between environments, and sharing folders reduce the friction of using two operating systems. You can share your Desktop and Downloads folders or choose specific working folders, rather than maintain duplicate copies of everything.
Parallels also lets the Windows VM use your keyboard and mouse, camera, and microphone. When you connect a USB storage device, it asks whether to attach it to your Mac or the VM.
For more sensitive work, you can isolate the VM instead of sharing Mac files and data. That is an important control: convenience and separation serve different purposes, and the sharing settings deserve attention when you first configure Windows.
Virtual machines and developer tools

				
					

				
			
Parallels 20 brought AI to Windows on a Mac.

Foundry




Parallels lets you create multiple virtual machines, making it useful for developers who need different operating systems or test configurations. The Configuration window provides control over CPU and memory allocation.
Snapshots preserve a VM’s state so you can return to it after experimenting with a beta application or changing a test environment. They make it easier to recover from an unsuccessful change without rebuilding the machine.
Pro also includes a command-line tool, prlctl, for managing VMs from scripts, and advanced networking controls for development and testing. 
Standard vs. Pro, Business, and Enterprise

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Choose the edition according to the work you need to do:


EditionWho should consider it?Main distinction

StandardHome users, students, and people running everyday Windows softwareUp to 4 virtual CPU cores and 8GB of memory per VM; annual or one-time purchase options
ProDevelopers and people with demanding workloadsHigher resource limits, development tools, and advanced configuration; subscription only
BusinessTeams and organizationsCentralized licensing and administration, with Jamf and Intune deployment integration
EnterpriseIT-managed deploymentsA management portal, policy controls, and organizational sign-on and provisioning capabilities

 



The limits refer to resources assigned to a VM, not extra hardware supplied by Parallels. Your Mac still needs enough capacity for macOS and your other applications.
Price and value for money
Standard is available as an annual subscription or a one-time purchase. Pro, Business, and Enterprise require subscriptions. Updates are included during an active subscription; a one-time license does not include upgrades to future major versions.


EditionAnnual subscriptionOne-time purchase

Standard$99.99 / £89.99 (currently $59.49 / £49.49)$219.99 / £154.99
Pro$119.99 / £99.99 (currently $64.99 / £54.99)Not available
Business$149.99 / £119.99Not available
EnterpriseContact ParallelsNot available

 Windows licensing is separate.



The one-time option may appeal if you only need a stable Windows setup occasionally, but it should not be treated as a promise of indefinite compatibility with future versions of macOS.
Subscriptions also include Parallels Toolbox and round-the-clock support. Eligible students and educators can receive discounts of up to 50%.
The overall cost depends on whether you also need to buy Windows. If you already have an eligible license, that changes the calculation. If you need a new one, include it in your budget rather than comparing Parallels’ price in isolation.
For occasional use, compare the cost with the alternatives in our best virtual machine software guide. CrossOver is another option for supported Windows applications and games, and does not require a Windows license.
Should you buy Parallels Desktop?
Parallels Desktop is a strong choice if Windows is an essential part of your work and you want it to fit comfortably into a Mac workflow. Straightforward setup, Coherence mode, and flexible VM controls make it useful both to people who need a single Windows application and to developers maintaining several environments.
Standard should be the starting point for everyday applications. Pro makes more sense when you need its development tools or additional resources. Business and Enterprise are aimed at organizations that need deployment and management controls.
Its weaknesses are cost and compatibility at the demanding end of Windows software, especially games. Version 27’s graphics improvements broaden its appeal to professional users, but they do not make it a universal replacement for a Windows PC.
Use the trial to check your essential software on your own Mac. If it runs well and Windows is something you rely on regularly, Parallels remains our leading virtualization recommendation.
 FAQ 


1.
Can you use Parallels for Mac for free?
The Parallels website offers a 14-day free trial so that you can see how Parallels Desktop works before buying the full version. Just remember that, if you don’t already have a valid license, you do still need to buy a license for Windows 11 Pro or Enterprise, which starts at a rather hefty $199.99/£219.99.





2.
Can you use Parallels Desktop on more than one Mac? 
No, you cannot use a single Parallels Desktop license on more than one Mac at the same time. According to Parallels’ licensing terms, each installation requires its own license.
If you are just moving to a new Mac, you can uninstall the software on the first Mac and install it on the new Mac.





3.
Does Parallels Desktop include a Windows license?
No, Parallels Desktop does not include a Windows license. You need to purchase a Windows license separately to use it. 
You need a Windows 11 Pro or Enterprise license. The less expensive Home edition of Windows 11 isn’t supported on Apple silicon Macs. A Windows 11 Pro license starts at around $199.99/£219.99. 
Parallels makes the process straightforward. Since version 18, it has allowed you to download and buy the ARM version of Windows 11 directly within the software. When you create a new virtual machine, you simply click a button labeled “Get Windows 11 from Microsoft,” and Parallels handles the download. You can then purchase a license through the Microsoft Store within the virtual machine, or use an existing Windows 11 license if you have one.
This is a significant advantage, as the ARM version of Windows isn’t normally sold directly to individual consumers – Parallels’ partnership with Microsoft is what makes this possible.





4.
Can you run Windows and macOS at the same time?
Yes, absolutely. Parallels Desktop is specifically designed to let you run Windows and macOS simultaneously, side by side, without needing to reboot your Mac.
Here’s how it works in practice:
Side-by-side windows: You can have your Windows desktop running in a window on your Mac desktop, alongside your normal Mac apps.
Coherence mode: For even deeper integration, Parallels offers a feature called Coherence mode. This mode lets Windows apps run alongside Mac apps as if they were native. You can even pin Windows apps to your Mac’s Dock.
Seamless interaction: Shared folders, drag-and-drop, and copy-and-paste between the two operating systems work effortlessly.
The only real trade-off is that your Mac is effectively running two operating systems at once, so it benefits from having plenty of RAM – Parallels recommends 16GB or more for the best experience.





5.
Can you buy Parallels Desktop without a subscription?
Yes, you can buy Parallels Desktop without a subscription. The Standard Edition is available as a perpetual license for a one-time fee, though the price has increased significantly in recent years.
As of the latest edition, the perpetual license for the Standard Edition costs $219.99/£154.99. This one-time fee allows you to use the software indefinitely without any recurring subscription, but upgrades to future major versions will cost extra.

title: iPhone Duo Compromises: Everything You Have to Give Up
content:
Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo asks buyers to pay more for a folding screen while accepting almost 40 compromises compared with the iPhone 18 Pro and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max, spanning camera capabilities, everyday usability, and ownership costs.


At equivalent storage capacities, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ costs $800 more than the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and $700 more than the Pro Max. Its main attraction is a radically different design: a 5.4-inch outer display opens into a 7.6-inch inner display, providing more space for reading and viewing content, with the ability to use apps side by side.

MagSafe, and USB-C with USB 3 speeds. However, choosing the foldable means giving up some familiar features and accepting differences in how the phone feels, works, and fits into a daily routine.

General Compromises

The general compromises concern the phone's controls, displays, dimensions, battery life, and cost. Some change interactions that iPhone owners perform throughout the day, while others affect particular preferences or longer-term ownership expenses. When choosing the ‌iPhone Duo‌ over an ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ or Pro Max, users must be prepared to give up:


Face ID: Facial authentication is replaced by Touch ID in the side button, changing how users unlock their phone and authenticate purchases and apps.

The Action button: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ drops the customizable button used for functions such as Silent mode, the flashlight, Focus modes, and Shortcuts. Camera Control remains available, but there is no dedicated physical mute control.

MagSafe wallet compatibility: Apple lists ‌MagSafe‌ cases and wireless chargers as compatible with the ‌iPhone Duo‌, but omits the wallet compatibility it lists for the Pro models due to the device's shape.

Physical SIM support in some markets: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ is eSIM-only worldwide. Pro models sold in markets such as the UK and Australia retain a nano-SIM slot, giving buyers the option of using physical SIM cards.

A larger screen without unfolding: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer display measures 5.4 inches, compared with 6.3 inches on the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. Accessing its larger 7.6-inch screen requires opening the device.

The Pro displays' pixel density on the larger screen: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s inner display has a density of 430 pixels per inch, compared with 460 ppi on both Pro models. Its outer display retains 460 ppi.

A crease-free display: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s folding screen has a crease that remains visible in certain lighting, despite Apple's efforts to minimize it. The Pro models have a conventional display without a fold through the center.

Simpler display maintenance: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer screen has Ceramic Shield 2, while the inner screen uses a different construction with a polymer cover layer. That layer is replaceable if it wears or becomes damaged, introducing an additional service item absent from the Pro models. In the U.S., a cover-layer replacement costs $49 without AppleCare+ coverage or $19 with coverage.

A thinner, narrower, and lighter phone: Although shorter when closed, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is 84.1mm wide and 11.3mm thick, compared with widths of 71.9mm and 78mm and a thickness of 8.75mm on the Pro models. At 254 grams, it is also 43 grams heavier than the Pro and five grams heavier than the Pro Max.

The Pro Max's longer typical-use battery life: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ is rated for up to 24 hours of typical use, matching the smaller Pro but falling short of the Pro Max's 30 hours.

Longer video playback when using the larger display: With its inner screen, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is rated for up to 31 hours of video playback and 26 hours of streaming, compared with 36 and 33 hours on the Pro and 45 and 40 hours on the Pro Max. Using the outer display improves those figures to 44 and 37 hours, exceeding the smaller Pro's ratings.

Faster wired charging: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ reaches up to 50% charge in around 20 minutes, compared with around 15 minutes on both Pro models. 

Higher sustained-performance: Apple quotes up to 35% better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, compared with up to 40% for the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models.

More color choices: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ comes in Night Sky and Star White. The Pro models offer Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy.

A higher proportion of recycled content: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ contains 35% recycled content, compared with 40% on the Pro models.

A lower purchase price: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ costs $800 more than the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and $700 more than the Pro Max at equivalent storage capacities. Its $1,999 starting price buys 256GB, while a 1TB Pro Max costs $1,899.

Lower single-device AppleCare premiums: In the U.S., ‌AppleCare‌+ with Theft and Loss costs $19.99 per month or $199.99 annually for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, compared with $14.99 per month or $149.99 annually for either Pro model.

Lower covered screen-repair fees: Under U.S. ‌AppleCare‌ coverage, accidental damage to the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s inner display carries a $99 service fee, compared with $29 for screen-only damage on the Pro models. The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer-display damage fee remains $29.

Lower repair fees without AppleCare+ coverage: Apple's U.S. estimates include $999 for inner-display damage, compared with screen-repair fees of $329 for the Pro and $379 for the Pro Max. "Other damage" is estimated at $1,499, compared with $849 and $899 respectively. Back-glass repair is also more expensive, at $199 rather than $159 for either Pro model.

Lower battery replacement costs: Apple's U.S. out-of-warranty battery service fee is $229 for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, compared with $129 for either Pro model.



Face ID or the Action button may be more disruptive to an established routine than having fewer color choices, while the wider, thicker body is something buyers will encounter every time they pick up the closed phone. Buyers moving from a Pro Max also need to consider whether the larger inner display is worth giving up its longer typical-use battery life.

The financial differences extend beyond the initial purchase. Higher ‌AppleCare‌ premiums, repair fees, and battery replacement costs can increase the expense of owning the ‌iPhone Duo‌ over several years, so buyers should consider how they intend to maintain and protect the device alongside its purchase price.

Camera and Capture Compromises

The camera compromises range from fewer zoom options and simpler front cameras to the loss of professional capture formats. Some affect everyday photography, while others matter primarily to users with specific editing and production workflows. When buying the ‌iPhone Duo‌ over an ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ or Pro Max, customers must be prepared to forgo:



A dedicated Telephoto camera: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ lacks the Pro models' 48-megapixel 4x Telephoto camera, including its tetraprism design and 3D sensor-shift stabilization, and the 12-megapixel optical-quality 8x crop it enables. Its longest optical-quality zoom setting is a 2x crop from the Main camera. Digital photo zoom tops out at 10x rather than 40x, while video zoom reaches 6x rather than 24x.

A variable aperture: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s Main camera has a fixed f/1.6 aperture. The Pro models offer f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0 settings, giving users more control over light capture and depth of field.

The Pro Main camera's stabilization and focusing hardware: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ uses sensor-shift optical image stabilization and Hybrid Focus Pixels, compared with second-generation sensor-shift stabilization and 100% Focus Pixels on the Pro models.

Wider Main-camera framing: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s Main camera has a 26mm equivalent focal length rather than 24mm, producing a slightly tighter view. Its 2x crop is also tighter, at 52mm rather than 48mm.

A LiDAR Scanner: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ omits the depth-sensing hardware available on both Pro models for photography, augmented reality, and scanning experiences.

Adaptive True Tone flash: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has a standard True Tone flash instead of the Pro models' adaptive version.

Pro Controls: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ does not have the Pro models' full suite of aperture, shutter speed, white balance, and histogram controls.

ProRAW photography: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ does not offer Apple's ProRAW capture, including on its front camera.

Apple Reference Image capture: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ cannot capture the signed reference images used to help establish whether a photo has been altered.

Spatial photos and videos: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ cannot capture spatial photos or spatial video. Both Pro models support spatial video recording at 1080p at 30 fps.

ProRes and ProRes RAW recording: These professional video formats are unavailable in the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s native camera feature set, including for front-facing capture. The Pro models support ProRes recording up to 4K at 120 fps from the rear camera and 4K at 60 fps from the front camera with external recording.

Apple Log 2 and ACES: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ omits Apple Log 2 and Academy Color Encoding System support for rear and front-camera recording, limiting the professional color workflows otherwise available on the Pro models.

Genlock: The ‌iPhone Duo‌ lacks the Pro models' support for synchronizing video capture with other cameras using supported accessories.

Studio-quality four-mic array: Apple specifies four studio-quality microphones for the Pro models, but does not list the same specification for the ‌iPhone Duo‌. The foldable still supports Spatial Audio recording, wind noise reduction, and Audio Mix.

A higher-resolution outer front camera: The ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer Center Stage camera is 12 megapixels with a smaller f/2.2 aperture, compared with 18 megapixels and f/1.9 on the Pro models.

A fully featured front camera when unfolded: The inner under-display camera is limited to 1080p video at 30 or 60 fps and lacks Night mode, portrait photography, and Photographic Styles. The Pro models' front camera supports 4K Dolby Vision recording and these photography features.



The missing Telephoto camera is a practical limitation even for buyers who never use professional formats, since it reduces the options for photographing subjects they cannot get close to. The variable aperture adds another form of control over how a scene is captured. For users who already rely on ProRAW, ProRes, or Log recording, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ also changes what they can capture and how they can edit it afterward.

Are the Compromises Worth It?

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ can justify these compromises if its inner display meaningfully improves things you already do on your phone. Reading long articles, reviewing documents, comparing information in two apps, editing photos, or watching video could all become much more comfortable with a larger screen. If those are activities you would regularly unfold the device for, its defining feature could be more valuable to you than several of the capabilities it lacks.

iPad or Mac.

Hands-on demo time should also be helpful, and include time using the phone closed. Check whether you are comfortable with its width, thickness, weight, outer display, and ‌Touch ID‌ button, then unfold it and try the activities you expect to benefit from the larger screen. The device needs to suit both the quick interactions that make up much of phone use and the longer sessions that take advantage of its inner display.

The large number of compromises alone should not determine your decision. If you never record ProRes video, losing it may have no consequence, while giving up a telephoto camera you use every day could be decisive.

There is also value in being enthusiastic about Apple's radically new take on the iPhone. Wanting to explore a folding design and new ways of using familiar apps is a reasonable part of the buying decision, even without a specific productivity benefit.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ makes the most sense for buyers who expect to use its inner display frequently, enjoy adapting to the new form factor, and are comfortable with the features and money they give up to get it. For buyers who expect to spend most of their time on the outer display, or who place greater importance on camera versatility, the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models may be a stronger fit at a lower price.

title: iPhone 19 or iPhone 20? Apple’s 2027 anniversary iPhone rumors, specs and release date
content:
Macworld





The original iPhone was previewed in January 2007 and then released on June 29, 2007. So in 2027, it will turn 20 years old, and rumors point to Apple commemorating the event with a special 20th-anniversary model.
It’s not expected to launch on June 29 (it will probably be in September, as usual), and it may not be a special one-off product, but rather the next major evolution of the iPhone, much like the iPhone X in 2017. But either way, the big two-oh is supposed to bring something really special.
Will Apple call its next-generation models iPhone 19, or skip straight to iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary? Reports suggest the latter is possible, but the name remains unconfirmed. 
Here’s what we’ve gleaned from the rumors and leaks so far.
20th Anniversary iPhone: What to expect
Name: Unconfirmed; one report suggests Apple could skip iPhone 19 and use iPhone 20.
Major redesign: Apple is expected to mark the iPhone’s 20th anniversary in 2027 with a near-all-screen design, curved glass, ultra-thin bezels, and two Pro-sized models.
Display upgrades: Face ID could move under the display, leaving only a small punch-hole front camera for a cleaner look.
Key hardware improvements: Rumored upgrades include a new Sony camera sensor, solid-state haptic buttons, and a silicon-anode battery for better battery life.
More powerful internals: The phone is expected to feature a next generation chip; a C3 modem, and improved wireless connectivity for better performance and efficiency.
Timing and price: A fall 2027 launch is expected with a price of $1,299 or more.


Will Apple skip iPhone 19 and launch iPhone 20?

				
					

				
			
Steve Jobs demonstrating  the first iPhone in January 2007.

Apple




The iPhone that launches in 2027 will mark twenty years since the first iPhone was announced. What will this 20th-anniversary iPhone be called? iPhone 20 is one reported possibility, while iPhone XX remains a speculative alternative.
In October 2025, research firm Omdia reportedly predicted that Apple would skip the iPhone 19 name and move directly to iPhone 20. 
There is a precedent. For the iPhone’s tenth anniversary in 2017, Apple introduced the iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus alongside the iPhone X, skipping iPhone 9 entirely. The iPhone X brought an OLED display with no Home button, Face ID, and a then-record starting price of $999. It also supported wireless charging, which debuted on the iPhone 8 models that year.
Apple could take a similar approach in 2027, launching a standard iPhone 19 alongside a more expensive anniversary model called iPhone 20 – or another name entirely. The 2017 launch shows that Apple can depart from its numbering sequence, but neither the anniversary model’s name nor the possibility of an iPhone 19 launching alongside it is confirmed.


						

							


iPhone 19 or 20 release date: When will the 20th Anniversary iPhone launch?
Likely release date: September 2027
There has been no hard information on the 20th Anniversary iPhone’s release date yet, but it is generally expected to launch in the typical time frame for iPhones: an announcement in September and an on-sale in late September or October 2027.
An August 2026 report from a financial analyst at Jefferies claimed that Apple had canceled the all-glass anniversary iPhone because of manufacturing difficulties and concerns about its financial viability. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman disputed that report, saying Apple was still planning a glass-centric redesign for 2027, albeit with changes to its construction.


						

							


How much will the 20th Anniversary iPhone cost?
High starting price estimated at $1,299 or more
It’s too early to predict what the RAM crunch will do to next year’s prices, but we expect the 20th Anniversary iPhone to be expensive. With more advanced technology than most “Pro” iPhones, the starting price will likely be at least $1,299, if not more.


						

							


What will the 20th Anniversary iPhone look like?
Two sizes with slightly larger displays rumored
Edge-to-edge displays
Curved glass design
One of the defining visual characteristics of the 20th Anniversary iPhone will reportedly be its all-display look. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman claimed in May 2025 that Apple is planning an all-glass design.  Leaks have described the handset as having “a quad-curved screen design,” with the idea being that the phone will appear to be one big display. Bezels could be minimized to the point where you don’t even see them, and the glass will curve down on all four sides. It’s been reported that Apple could adopt its Liquid Glass branding as well.
“Glass-centric” doesn’t necessarily mean an entirely glass enclosure. According to Gurman’s August 2026 report, Apple encountered difficulties joining the front and back glass panels when preparing the design for mass production. The revised approach reportedly uses a metal band to connect them, while retaining glass that curves around all four sides.
Reports also suggest that Apple is preparing two anniversary models with slightly larger displays than the current Pro iPhones. According to leaker Digital Chat Station in July 2026, Apple is testing a 6.41-inch display with a resolution of approximately 2,686 × 1,236 pixels and a 6.96-inch display with approximately 2,912 × 1,340 pixels. The larger model could be marketed as having a 7-inch screen, potentially making it the largest display on a conventional, non-folding iPhone.


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have a Dynamic Island?
Under-display Face ID expected
Hole-punch camera for selfie cam rumored

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




One of the persistent rumors over the past several years is that Apple will continue to put more front camera system components under the display, until it’s all display with no cutouts at all.
That may be several years away, but at least some of the components might be able to go behind the OLED display. One rumor claims that Apple will use a “spliced micro-transparent glass,” which will allow it to put the IR emitter under the display, leaving just the regular camera and maybe the IR receiving camera in a cutout region. If the IR camera can effectively go under the display as well, the 20th Anniversary iPhone will have just a single round punch-hole camera in front but retain Face ID.
The Digital Chat Station leak from July 2026 also indicated that Apple is testing a smaller Dynamic Island-style hole-punch design. 
Analyst Ross Young suggested in a post on X back in January 2026 that a smaller Dynamic Island would remain through 2027. He believes Apple’s 2028 iPhone Pro models will feature a centered hole-punch cutout in the display.


						

							


What camera will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have?
Custom LOFIC image sensor rumored
Triple-camera array with telephoto lens

				
					

				
			
Stephan Wiesend




According to a Korean-language blog post by a leaker who goes by yeux1122 (who has been accurate in the past with some supply-chain scoops), Apple is working together with Sony on a custom image sensor that uses LOFIC (Lateral Integral Overflow Capacitor) technology.
Phone makers Honor, Xiaomi, and Huawei all use sensors with LOFIC technology in their flagship phones now. It’s a technique that allows sensors to capture low-light or dark areas of an image with less noise, along with brighter areas of an image, without increasing ISO sensitivity. In other words, it gives the camera more dynamic range with less noise.
Otherwise, we expect the 20th Anniversary iPhone to have a triple-camera system like the current Pro models, with wide, ultrawide, and telephoto cameras. It’s likely that the cameras will have significant upgrades, however, with a possible 200MP sensor.


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have physical buttons?
Solid-state with haptics could replace physical buttons

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




On all current MacBooks (other than MacBook Neo), the trackpad doesn’t actually move. Instead, it produces the sensation of being clicked using precise haptic feedback. It’s very effective and reduces the possibility of breakage due to fewer moving parts.
The 20th Anniversary iPhone is supposed to replace the power, volume, Action, and Camera Control buttons with parts that operate in a similar way. These buttons wouldn’t move at all. Rather, they will be integrated into the frame itself, but will have touch capacitors and haptics to give them the feel of an actual button.
Weibo account Instant Digital (with a mixed track record) says extensive testing is ongoing to make sure these new solid-state haptic buttons work well with gloves, cases, wet hands, and so on. 
If Apple can pull this off and they feel as good as real buttons, it will be an important part of the durability of the new iPhone. With the display glass curving down on all edges, the edge area of the frame itself will be very thin, and further cutouts to accommodate buttons would make it less likely to resist bending.


						

							


What specs will the 20th Anniversary iPhone 19 or 20 have?
A next-generation A-series processor is expected
A C3 modem has been rumored
RAM capacity remains unconfirmed
The 20th-anniversary iPhone is expected to feature a successor to the iPhone 18 Pro’s A20 Pro processor, potentially called A21 Pro. Apple has not announced the chip or its specifications.
Reports have suggested that Apple’s C3 cellular modem could arrive in 2027. The C2 is already used in the iPhone 18 Pro worldwide and in the iPhone 18 Pro Max outside the U.S.; the U.S. Pro Max uses Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80. Whether C3 will appear in every anniversary model remains unconfirmed.
Apple’s N1 wireless chip supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. It is too early to say whether the anniversary iPhone will retain N1 or introduce a successor.
RAM capacity is also unknown. Based on the iPhone 18 Pro, we would expect at least 12GB, while 16GB is a possibility if future features require more memory. This is our assessment rather than a confirmed specification or a sourced claim of a RAM increase.


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have longer battery life?
New battery technology
A report from ETNews in 2025 said that Apple is looking to use a battery with a pure silicon anode in the 20th Anniversary iPhone.
A silicon anode could increase energy density, allowing Apple to fit more battery capacity into the same space or use a smaller battery without sacrificing capacity. Some Android phones already demonstrate the potential of silicon-based batteries: the Oppo Find X9 Pro, for example, has a 7,500mAh silicon-carbon battery. That is different from the pure-silicon anode technology reportedly being considered for Apple’s anniversary iPhone. Apple’s battery capacity remains unknown, and any improvement in battery life would also depend on the display, processor, modem, and software.

title: Apple HomeView Includes Temperature and Humidity Sensors
content:

title: Is Siri AI coming to your big HomePod? Maybe but probably not
content:
Macworld





This week Apple launched the 2nd-gen HomePod mini, which features a more powerful S10 processor than the original model and a selection of new colors. But the most significant upgrade is its ability to run Siri AI, a far more capable voice assistant than the basic Siri which caused such issues when controlling previous HomePods.
Customers who already have multiple HomePods in their home now face a dilemma: should they upgrade to take advantage of Siri AI when it arrives on the new HomePod mini (Apple currently says only that it’s “coming in a future software update”), or stick with the older models, which remain excellent speakers? By all accounts, the new HomePod minis sound the same as the old model and look identical other than the new color options.
It’s a particularly tricky decision when it comes to the full-size HomePod, which has no new model to speak of. Switching from a full-sized HomePod to a new HomePod mini would be a downgrade in sound quality, even if it would be an upgrade in other ways.
If you’re about to pull the trigger on that latter purchase just to get the new Siri, we suggest you hold off just for now. Because a new and rather mysterious clue suggests Apple might be planning to bring Siri AI to the full-size HomePod, although it isn’t clear whether this would involve a software update, or a new model. Or, for that matter, whether this is actually just a simple misunderstanding or error.
At time of writing, if you go to the buy page for the full-size HomePod and scroll down a little, you’ll see a table comparing the features and price of this product and the new HomePod mini headlined “Which HomePod is right for you?” with pictures of the two devices. But, as spotted by the Twitter user pdfu and confirmed by Macworld, if you right-click on the image of the big HomePod and check the alt text, you’ll see the following:
HomePod, white color, full-size cylindrical design, seamless acoustic mesh exterior, multi-colored Siri AI glow on top.
How could the full-size HomePod have a “multi-colored Siri AI glow” when it doesn’t support Siri AI? It’s all rather mysterious. And may, we should stress, just be an error by someone who recently updated the site to reflect the HomePod mini’s new capabilities.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




But there is a real issue here. Right now it’s hard to see how Apple could possibly expect to sell the full-size HomePod. At $349, it costs more than twice as expensive as the new HomePod mini, even with the latest price hike, and officially doesn’t support Siri AI. It’s even more expensive than the new HomeView, which has a whole display attached to it. But more importantly, original Siri is really bad on the HomePod. Siri AI such an obvious and necessary step forward, that it’s tempting to regard the HomePod 2 as pretty much obsolete. Apple needs to announce an upgrade, or give up on the product entirely.
HomePod owners, or at least 2nd-gen HomePod owners, will be hoping this upgrade can be achieved through a free software update, but this is probably a false hope.
If we examine the official hardware requirements for Siri AI, we see that you need an iPhone or iPad with an A17 Pro or later, a Mac with an M1 or later, or, most crucially, an Apple Watch with an S9 or later. The HomePod mini has just been bumped from an S5 to an S10 processor, so it’s fine. But the full-size HomePod has an S7, which doesn’t have a Neural Engine. It just doesn’t seem like it would be capable of running anything other than a severely cut-down version of Siri AI.
At some point, I suspect, Apple will either announce a HomePod 3 or discontinue the full-size HomePod all over again. If it’s the first option, unfortunately, this is unlikely to happen soon, or Apple would have surely rolled this announcement in with the rest of Tuesday’s “Welcome Home” experience. So ultimately–and I would love to be wrong about this–the bold claim in the full-size HomePod’s alt text is probably just a mistake.

Is It Worth Upgrading From HomePod Mini to HomePod Mini 2?

For most existing ‌HomePod‌ mini owners, there is no general-purpose reason to replace a working original ‌HomePod‌ mini immediately. Sound Glow and the new finishes may appeal to enthusiasts, but they are very small reasons to replace speakers throughout a home. 

For buyers primarily interested in sound quality, Apple's specifications provide limited grounds for judging the size of the improvement. title: Every new Apple product coming in 2026 & 2027
content:
Macworld





It’s been a huge year for Apple, with a wave of new products arriving throughout 2026. The year began with the MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e in March, followed by the new Mac mini and Mac Studio in August.
September brought another major wave of launches at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.
Then on October 13 the company held a “Welcome Home” gathering at which new smart-home products debuted including HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a new Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection.
Apple has also rolled out its major operating-system updates for 2026, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, alongside updates for the Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro.
But Apple isn’t finished yet. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that further Mac and iPad announcements are planned for October 27, although Apple has yet to confirm that date.
With most of Apple’s biggest launches already behind us, attention is turning to what’s next. Here’s what’s still to come.
Apple’s roadmap: At a glance
As of September 1, 2026, Apple’s roadmap has come under the direction of CEO John Ternus. Former CEO Tim Cook has moved into the executive chairman role. The shift from an operations-focused leader to one with deep hardware engineering roots could signal a more product-driven approach – and a renewed emphasis on standout hardware.

Every New Apple Product Launched in 2026… so far
Here is what Apple has already announced in 2026:
HomeView: A new smart-home display with a 7-inch touchscreen, available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions.
HomePod mini 2: An updated speaker with an S10 chip, new colors and Siri AI coming through a future software update.
Apple TV 4K: A fourth-generation model with an A19 chip and an updated Siri Remote.
Apple Home Collection: Cameras, doorbells, locks and thermostats developed with accessory partners.
iPhone Duo: Apple’s first foldable iPhone: iPhone Duo Guide.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: A20 Pro chip, upgraded vapor-chamber cooling, camera improvements: iPhone 18 Pro & Max Guide.
Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4: Faster chips, Apple’s latest health-sensing features: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4.
AirPods 5: Stronger open-ear Active Noise Cancellation and longer battery life: AirPods 5.
Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro: Faster storage, upgraded connectivity, and a strong focus on AI performance: New Mac mini 2026 guide.
Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Faster AI and graphics performance, increased memory bandwidth: New Mac Studio 2026 guide.
AirPods Max 2: Improved audio and the H2 chip. Find out more here: AirPods Max 2 guide.
MacBook Neo: Apple’s brand new, low-cost Mac laptop. Find out more here: MacBook Neo guide.
MacBook Air M5: Now with the M5 chip. Read about the 2026 MacBook Air here: MacBook Air M5 guide.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro & M5 Max: A significant upgrade over the M4 series. Read: MacBook Pro M5 Pro & Max guide.
Studio Display: Finally gets Thunderbolt 5 and a better webcam. 
Studio Display XDR: With mini-LED technology and ProMotion up to 120Hz.
iPhone 17e: The new, entry-level, iPhone replaces the iPhone 16e. Read more here: iPhone 17e guide.
iPad Air M4: The iPad Air now has an M4 chip. Read more here: iPad Air M4 guide.
AirTag 2: Four years on Apple updated the AirTag, read our review here: AirTag 2nd gen review.
And… RIP Mac Pro: Apple has confirmed that it is discontinuing its tower workstation.  
Read on to find out what new products to expect at Apple’s next event and throughout 2026.


						

							







Every New Apple Product Launching in 2026
In the sections below we’ve split the upcoming new products into categories including Mac, iPad, iPhone, Apple Watch, Home, AirPods, and some new product categories.
Apple Intelligence and Siri updates still coming in 2026
Apple released iOS 27, iPadOS 27 and its other major software updates in September, bringing the new Siri AI experience, expanded Apple Intelligence features, parental controls and a range of improvements across Apple’s apps and operating systems.
But Apple’s 2026 software rollout isn’t finished. Siri AI is still being rolled out to eligible users, with access depending on device, language and region, and Apple has already begun testing the updates that will follow the initial iOS 27 and macOS 27 releases.
Siri and Apple Intelligence
Siri AI arrived with iOS 27 as a substantially redesigned version of Apple’s voice assistant, with improved conversational abilities, personal-context awareness, onscreen awareness and the ability to carry out more actions across apps. However, not every Apple device can run the new features, and some users may still need to join a waiting list before gaining access.
Apple is also expanding Siri AI beyond its initial English-language launch. Additional language support is due during the remainder of 2026, while regional restrictions mean some Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features remain unavailable in parts of the world. 
Upcoming iOS 27 and macOS updates
iOS 27 itself is already available, but Apple is continuing development through iOS 27.x updates. These releases are expected to deliver additional features, refinements and bug fixes throughout the remainder of 2026, with Apple’s beta program providing an early indication of what is coming next.
The same applies to iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27 and Apple’s other platforms, which will continue to receive point updates following their initial September releases. Find out about the latest iOS beta and latest macOS beta.  


						

							


What new iPads are coming in 2026/2027 

				
					

				
			
Screenshot

Foundry




Don’t expect major redesigns for the iPads this year. Instead, Apple is likely to focus on faster chips and other internal upgrades. That said, both the iPad and iPad mini are due for an update – particularly the entry-level iPad, which currently lacks support for Apple Intelligence. Here’s what we expect Apple to announce:
iPad mini
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.
The next iPad mini could be one of Apple’s biggest remaining upgrades of the year. Multiple reports point to Apple replacing the current 8.3-inch LCD with an OLED display, potentially increasing the screen size slightly to around 8.5 inches while keeping the overall dimensions much the same. Samsung Display is also reported to have begun mass-producing OLED panels for the new model, suggesting the launch is getting closer.
The latest reporting points to the A20 Pro chip – as used in the iPhone 18 Pro. Earlier references suggested the A19 Pro, but more recent findings in Apple code favor the newer processor. 
Other upgrades could include Apple’s N1 networking chip, bringing Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread, while cellular models are expected to adopt Apple’s C1X modem. Apple may also move the front camera to the landscape edge, bringing the iPad mini into line with the rest of the current iPad range.
Apple is also reportedly working on a more water-resistant design. Bloomberg has reported that this could involve a new vibration-based speaker system that would allow Apple to eliminate conventional speaker holes and improve sealing. Bloomberg points to an October 27 announcement, although Apple has not confirmed the date. Read our round up of iPad mini rumors.
iPad 
Late 2026 update possible
When the standard iPad was updated in March 11, 2025, the biggest disappointment was that it featured a A16 chip and therefore didn’t support Apple Intelligence. Apple looks set to rectify that in 2026 with an upgrade to the A18 or A19 chip, with the latter offering 50% better performance. The release timeline for an iPad with an A18 or A19 chip is anticipated before the end of 2026, in fact, Apple code suggests the company may be planning an update sooner-rather-than-later.
Read more about the 2026 iPad in our rumor round up. 
Should you buy now or wait? 
With the iPad prices increasing in June 2026, you may want to hold off buying one now. If you are going to pay more at least get the most up-to-date model, or buy from Apple’s Refurbished Store to get a bargain. Read Should I buy an iPad now or wait?


						

							


Which new Macs are coming in 2026/2027?
2026 is expected to be a significant year for the Mac, with Apple’s first touchscreen Mac rumored as part of a MacBook Pro redesign. March 3 saw the launch of the M5 MacBook Air and M5 Pro/M5 Max MacBook Pro and March 4 saw Apple introduce a new entry-level laptop – the $599 MacBook Neo.
The long expected Mac Studio and Mac mini updates came in August 2026 and went on sale September 22, although some high-memory Mac Studio configurations won’t arrive until later. These Macs have become popular for running AI models locally; however, global RAM shortages – driven by AI companies purchasing large amounts of memory for data centres – have been having a knock-on effect on availability during 2026 and these RAM shortages have also had an effect on prices, with Mac prices increasing by $300 to $500 in June and in the case of the Mac mini, by a further $100 with the 2026 launch.
One Mac that won’t be getting an update is the long-neglected Mac Pro. Apple has confirmed that the Mac Pro will be discontinued in favor of the Mac Studio.
Touchscreen MacBook Pro
Expected announcement: October 27, according to Bloomberg; unconfirmed.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is expected to feature an OLED touchscreen and a substantially lighter body. However, Mark Gurman has played down earlier suggestions that it will be significantly thinner. Reports point to the use of M5 Pro and M5 Max processors to enable Apple to keep the project on schedule.

Apple is expected to update the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip. This would be a separate update from the rumored OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
Gurman includes this model among the products reportedly planned for October 27.

iMac

Apple is reportedly preparing an M6 iMac, skipping the M5 generation following the M4 model introduced in October 2024. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman expects the update before the end of 2026, with new color options but no major redesign.
