title: Apple Home Collection is an expensive way to build your smart home
content:
Macworld





Apple made its big Welcome Home smart home pitch on Tuesday, in which it introduced the new HomeView device, along with upgrades to the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini. But for anyone worried that there aren’t enough smart home devices that support Apple’s ecosystem (either HomeKit or Matter), there’s also a suite of new smart home gadgets from LG and Schneider Electric.
The Apple Home Collection consists of a set of six items from LG and one item from Schneider Electric. They are not Apple-branded, but have been “designed in collaboration” with Apple and will no doubt be sold in Apple Stores when they become available in December (with some items coming in early 2027).
They appear to be, generally, a little more expensive than comparable smart home items with comparable specs from other brands, but we have yet to see if you can reliably find them on sale at online retailers. Here’s the product list with their retail prices:
LG Video Doorbell: Dual cameras (front and downward to see packages) and a built-in spotlight, with resolution up to 2.5K. $249.95/£229.95 at the Apple Store.
LG Floodlight Cam: Dual motion-activated floodlights and low-light color night vision with camera resolution up to 2.5K. $399.95/£349.95 at the Apple Store.
LG Outdoor Cam: Also offers low-light color vision and 2.5K resolution, but without the floodlights, and with easy self-installation. $299.95/£279.95 at the Apple Store.
LG Indoor Cam: A 2.5K motorized camera that tilts up when you’re away, and points downward when you’re home to protect your privacy. $199.95/£179.95 at the Apple Store.
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock: Using Ultra Wideband, it can detect when a user that has a compatible Home Key on their iPhone is walking up and unlock automatically. You can always tap your iPhone, Apple Watch, use the PIN keypad, or a physical key. $349.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).
LG Smart Thermostat: What can you say? It’s a circular smart thermostat that supports the Apple Home thermostat features like Adaptive Temperature. $199.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).
Schneider Home Smart Thermostat: The same sort of thing as the LG Smart Thermostat, only with more of a “rounded square” sort of design. $199.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).
There are LG and Schneider temperature sensors for other rooms available for $39.95, and some accessories like trim plates and C-wire power adapters.
Of the group, the thermostats seem almost unnecessary. There are a good number of smart home thermostats that support the Matter protocol and therefore work just fine with Apple’s home control and with Siri. Home security cameras that support Apple HomeKit Secure Video are more rare, primarily just from the brands Aqara and Eve. Smart locks that support Apple’s ecosystem are similarly pretty easy to come by with popular brands like Yale, Schlage, Level, and Aqara.
Since the LG cameras use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, no extra subscription is required, but the number of cameras supported by HKSV is dependent on your iCloud+ plan. If you have a 50GB plan, it supports a single camera only. The 200GB plan works with up to 5 cameras, and the 2TB plan supports unlimited cameras.
If you want to use Apple Intelligence with these cameras to get smart descriptions and notifications, that’s on a whole other level: you need the 2TB plan to get Apple Intelligence features on a single camera, the 6TB plan for up to 2 cameras, and the 12TB plan to support up to 5 cameras. That’s $59.99 a month in iCloud+ storage subscription fees to get AI summaries on five cameras.

title: Apple Launches 'Apple Home Collection' With Cameras, Lock, Thermostats and More

Apple today debuted the "Apple Home Collection," an accessory lineup it developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The collection includes cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, and a door lock.


All of the home devices are designed to work with the HomeView, Apple's new home hub. Apple says each one is made from premium materials with a minimal aesthetic. The accessories are able to be set up with a single tap from the iPhone, and can be controlled with the Home app and through Siri.

 	
LG Video Doorbell ($249.95) - The Video Doorbell has dual cameras that capture views of visitors and packages. The front camera has a 2.5K resolution and the bottom camera is HD resolution. It has a built-in spotlight and a chime that plays through HomeView, HomePod, or ‌HomePod‌ mini.

The tilt function works based on geofencing, but can also be controlled in the Home app or manually.

The thermostat can read temperature and humidity across multiple rooms using separate temperature and humidity sensors. Sensors are priced at $39.95.

 	
Schneider Electric Thermostat ($199.95) - Also supports Adaptive Temperature and can be used with temperature and humidity sensors. Sensors are priced at $39.95.


iCloud+ plans and users can view live footage and camera activity from the Home app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV 4K, and HomeView.

title: New Apple TV 4K Supports Surround Sound via Four HomePods
content:
As was rumored prior to today's announcements, the new Apple TV 4K can connect to up to four HomePods in front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right positions, enabling an all-Apple surround sound system for home theater setups.


You can connect four of the new HomePod mini 2 speakers to the new Apple TV 4K, or you can mix and match pairs of HomePod mini 2 and full-sized HomePod 2 speakers, so long as the front and rear pairs of speakers match. Apple is relying on computational audio. The company says the four HomePods and the new Apple TV 4K can "intelligently recognize each speaker's position in the room, so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space."

All previous Apple TV 4K models remain limited to two HomePods for stereo sound.

title: HomeView first look: Apple’s adorable new smart hub oozes personality
content:
Macworld





Apple’s newest device isn’t an Apple Watch or an iPhone or even an iPad—but it has elements of all three. Called HomeView, it’s a “personal” smart display designed to be the centerpiece of your home. The screen looks something like a giant Apple Watch, but it’s an entirely new device designed to be touched like an iPad, spun like an iMac G4, and spoken to like a smart speaker, all wrapped up in an adorable package that’s equally at home on a kitchen counter or end table.
You can scroll through the images below to see it in real life, but I wanted to spotlight a couple here too. When mounted on a wall with the wire hidden (no easy task), it looks elegant and futuristic, almost like a visionOS widget. It’s a little thick at nearly 10mm, but the brushed metal case and rounded corners add a sophistication you won’t get with an Echo Show.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Of course, most people will opt for the base-attached HomeView, which is actually cheaper than the wall-mounted model when you factor in the cost of a mount and installation. And it’s adorable. It looks something like a mini robot, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see it gain wheels and the ability to automatically swivel when it hears a voice call for Siri. (Honest: Apple is already working on a device that can do that, and this design seems tailor-made for it.)

				
					

				
			
Foundry




It definitely has personality. There’s a little throwback to the iMac G4 in its design, but it’s also updated to fit today’s aesthetic. The only downside is that it needs to stay near an outlet, so it can’t really exist in the center of a table like Apple is demonstrating in its ads. But I’m kind of in love with its stubby little shape and can’t get enough of its cute footprint. I’ll be buying one.
Text by Michael Simon. All images by Britta O’Boyle for Macworld.

title: HomeView Can Dim to Apple's Lowest-Ever Display Brightness
content:
The HomeView can dim its display to just 0.3 nits for use on a nightstand or in dark environments, making it Apple's lowest-ever display brightness.


The 7-inch Liquid Retina display automatically adjusts its brightness as lighting conditions change, reaching up to 500 nits in bright rooms. Its 0.3-nit minimum allows it to dim substantially at night. True Tone also helps the screen adapt to changing ambient light.

Previously, Apple's dimmest display technology went down to just 1 nit. This feature debuted on the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2, and subsequently came to the iPhone.

The tabletop HomeView model features a stainless steel hinge that lets users tilt the display as required. Its interface responds to distance, showing simpler information from across the room and more detail as users move closer.

The HomeView also offers customizable faces, including weather information, photos, and animated designs. Apple says selected faces change throughout the day, adapting their appearance for mornings and evenings.

title: New Apple TV 4K Adds Far-Field Microphones for Hands-Free Siri
content:
Apple's new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K includes three built-in far-field microphones, allowing users to find something to watch and control playback without picking up the Siri Remote.


Users can activate the voice assistant by saying "Hey ‌Siri‌" or "‌Siri‌," including while a movie or TV show is playing. Apple says advanced echo cancellation separates the user's voice from background sound, helping the device recognize requests over the TV's audio.

The microphones also enable hands-free control of compatible smart home accessories and scenes. With ‌Siri‌ AI, users can search for entertainment conversationally and ask follow-up questions about what they are watching, with answers appearing in a compact overlay over the video.

Apple TV 4K and its A19 chip include Secure Exclaves, which are protected processing environments that handle microphone data separately from the rest of the system. According to Apple, data processed and analyzed inside these environments cannot be accessed by tvOS, apps, users, or Apple itself.

Far-field ‌Siri‌ support varies by region and language. The feature is supported when the primary tvOS language is set to English, Mandarin Chinese, Dutch, Finnish, French, German, Hebrew, Norwegian, or Swedish.

title: Apple Details HomeView's Audio Hardware
content:
Apple's new HomeView supports Spatial Audio, with different speaker systems for its tabletop and wall-mounted models.


The tabletop model features two custom full-range drivers in its display, with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators housed in the domed base. Apple says this arrangement delivers clear sound with extended bass, distributing the audio hardware between the screen and its stand.

The HomeView's A18 chip and built-in sensors power computational audio that continuously adjust loudness and bass response. According to Apple, this processing helps maintain consistent, balanced sound at different volume levels.

The wall-mounted HomeView uses two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for placement on a wall, but lacks the added speaker hardware in the tabletop models' base. It still supports Spatial Audio.


For music playback, HomeView supports multiroom audio alongside other HomeView devices, HomePod, HomePod mini, and AirPlay-compatible speakers. Handoff lets users transfer music from an iPhone by placing it in front of the HomeView's display. Apple Music displays animated album artwork and lyrics, while Apple Podcasts and compatible third-party audio apps can provide additional content.

Siri requests and FaceTime calls. Apple says the microphone array can pick up voices from across the room while reducing background noise.

title: HomeView's Wall Model: Pay More, Get Less Speaker
content:
Apple offers two versions of the HomeView, one that can be mounted on the wall and one that's a standalone model with a speaker base. The wall-mounted version and the speaker version are both priced at $299, with no discount for the base-free model.


Wall mounting is the more expensive option because most buyers will need hardware that's sold separately and is currently priced starting at $60. There are three options for mounting the HomeView on the wall.

 	
Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector ($59.95) - The USB-C mount is from Schneider Home, and Apple says it is a self-install mount. It uses a standard USB-C cable that goes to a power adapter, which the user also needs to supply. It requires a 20W or higher power adapter.

 	
Power Mount AC Wired ($79.95) - The AC Wired mount uses in-wall power so there's no visible cable. Apple recommends having it installed by a licensed electrician and is partnering with ADT to offer installation services.

 	
Power Mount PoE Wired ($129.95) - The Power over Ethernet hardwired mount is not available right now. Apple says to check back later for availability. It will require a home with PoE wiring.

 	
No mount - There is an option to buy the wall-mounted version with no additional hardware. Presumably, accessory companies will eventually offer mounting solutions, but Apple has the only mount option right now.


In addition to being more expensive, the wall-mounted HomeView comes in more limited color options. It can only be purchased in silver or space gray, while the speaker version also comes in starlight and rose pink.

Both HomeView models have speakers with "two custom full-range drivers" in the display, and the wall-mounted version uses computational audio tuned for on-wall placement. The model with a speaker base also has a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators that are not available in the wall-mounted version.

We'll need to wait for reviews to see sound comparisons on the speaker version and the wall-mounted version, but customers who opt for the wall-mounted version are going to be paying more for less hardware.

title: Welcome Home live blog: HomeView hub, Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini, and more!
content:
Macworld





Today (Tuesday, October 13) at 9 am ET, Apple launched a new crop of products as part of its Welcome Home launch. While we didn’t get a proper keynote presentation to announce the new stuff, there is a lot to see, with no fewer than three new products and a whole bunch of new features and accessories. Follow along with us!
Apple Welcome Home Launch Live Blog


1 day ago, By David Price
Are more announcements on the way?
The last time we did an Apple experience (not event!) was for the launch of the MacBook Neo in March. But the interesting thing then was the way Apple spread the announcements across three days: iPad Air and iPhone 17e on Monday, MacBooks Air and Pro on Tuesday, and finally the MacBook Neo on Wednesday.
I’m sorry to tell you this but it’s very unlikely that Apple has something similar planned for this week. Today’s raft of home products are almost certainly all we’re getting until later in the month (most likely the 27th), when we’re expecting the M6 MacBook Pro, the M6 iMac, a new touchscreen MacBook, and the next iPad mini. That might be split across multiple days. But the Welcome Home announcements are probably more of a one-day type of thing.

					
						

						Link copied
						

							SHARE
						


							


1 day ago, By David Price
You can't say squarer than that
It always takes a while to get used to the design of a completely new Apple product. But right now I feel like the HomeView looks weird. And I think it’s because it’s square… or a squircle, technically, because of the rounded corners. 
Everyone knows that the squircle was Steve Jobs’ favorite shape, which is why it crops up so much in Apple software design. But it crops up less often in the company’s hardware design, and almost never in the screen. Until now it was just the Apple Watch, which is why Wired described the HomeView as a “giant Apple Watch for the home.” 
Screens are expected to be rectangular. That’s why the iPhone Duo looks the way it does. Again, we get used to these things, but at one stage the Duo was called “weird,” “so strange,” and “a little shorty!” It needed to be stubbier than most smartphones so that, when it was unfolded, its screen would be rectangular rather than square.
Apple could very easily have given the HomeView a rectangular screen, so we have to believe the company thinks square is best in this specific use case. You’re not going to be watching movies or TV shows, or playing games. You’re not going to be reading eBooks or lengthy online articles. The screen is just there to let you view your home tech and control it with a few taps, chat to people using FaceTime, and look up the odd recipe. It’s a screen that plays far less of a role than that of an iPhone or a Mac. It really is more like the screen on an Apple Watch.

An early start
Some of you, particularly those of you based in the U.S., may be wondering why today’s launch is scheduled to start so early. (If you’re wondering how I’ve been manning the live blog for so long, by the way, rest assured that I’m in London and got up at the usual time today. This is fine.) The usual policy is for full events to start at 10 am Pacific Time, but the “Welcome Home” announcements will begin at 9 am Eastern Time, a full four hours earlier. What gives?
Well, first of all let’s be clear that those start times haven’t always been completely rigid. The “Let Loose” event in May 2024 started at 7 am PT, almost as early as this one; by contrast the “Scary Fast” event in October 2023 began at 5 pm PT and was a nighttime event. And way back in 2002, the Macworld Expo took place in New York at 9 am Eastern. Apple is happy enough to be flexible when it’s convenient.
But the main thing to remember is that this isn’t a full event. It’s an “experience,” the next level down from a full live-streamed event but one level up from a simple website update. The last one of those was the launch of the MacBook Neo in March, and that also happened at 9 am. This is standard practice for these kinds of launch. 
Maybe Apple likes to keep us on our toes; maybe it wants to get the news out before the New York Stock Exchange opens at 9.30 am ET (that’s my colleague Karen’s theory). Maybe John Ternus is just a naturally early bird. Whatever the reason, this means we have even longer to talk about the new products, and you have even longer to enjoy our post-announcement analysis here on the live blog.

Threading the needle
Apple fans love poring over the company’s event invitations, examining the tagline and artwork for clues to the upcoming announcements. Invites and pre-event marketing materials for the iPhone 17 launch event last year, for instance, contained hints about the device’s design, colors, and thermal cooling system. “Awe Dropping” indeed.
Compare that to the invites for today’s announcements and it’s hard not to feel a little disappointed. “Welcome Home” for an event focused on smart-home tech is about as unambiguous and straightforward as it’s possible for a tagline to be. The embroidered Apple logo probably doesn’t give away anything about the design or colors of the new products, which are more likely to be shiny aluminum than rustic cotton and wool; those are just the traditional Apple colors, in a new form.
And what of the embroidery itself? Is Apple making a comment about the old-fashioned craftsmanship involved in developing its products? Is it consciously creating a serene, homely atmosphere to play down the cold anonymity (not to mention the privacy concerns) of modern smart-home tech? Possibly. 
But here’s another possibility: it might be a reference to Thread, a low-power networking protocol used for the smart home and the internet of things. (Thread is closely associated with Matter, a standard designed to ensure compatibility between different companies’ smart-home products. My colleague Jason has written a primer on the two technologies.) Apple joined the Thread Group way back in 2018 and supports the standard across its product range, including the HomePod mini and Apple TV… and presumably the HomeView as well.

But don’t sleep on the expected update to the HomePod mini, which is both interesting and important in its own right.
The HomePods are excellent speakers, but very bad smart speakers, and that comes down to the shortcomings of Siri. On other devices, such as the iPhone and Apple Watch, Siri’s failings are an annoyance, but not a dealbreaker; you can control those devices through other means. But the HomePod relies on voice control to a greater extent than any other Apple product. And when Siri misunderstands your request to play a particular song time and time again, there’s not much you can do except swear and suppress the urge to throw the HomePod out the window.
Apple wants to put Siri’s bad old days behind it, thanks to the long-awaited arrival of Siri AI and its greater capabilities. But existing HomePod models can’t be updated to run Siri AI. Which is why a new version of the HomePod mini which has a processor capable of running Siri AI, even if it offers virtually nothing else (other than new colors), will be a timely and crucial launch. title: The new HomePod mini 2 is a bigger upgrade than it looks
content:
Macworld





Apple has announced the HomePod mini 2, an update to its smart speaker that was originally released six years ago. That’s a long time between updates–with a gap that long, this update should be a substantial one.
The HomePod mini 2 still has the same size and shape as the original HomePod mini, but it does have substantial-enough upgrades that you’ll want to replace your original HomePod mini if you have one. And if you’re new to the HomePod mini 2, you should know the new features, in case you’re thinking of getting by with an old one you might find at a cheap price. Here’s what the new HomePod mini 2 can do that the original HomePod mini doesn’t.
Siri AI
This is probably the reason why it took four years for the HomePod mini 2 to hit the market. Siri AI is Apple’s voice-activated digital assistant, and on the HomePod mini 2, think of it as a competitor to Amazon’s Alexa or Google Home. The new model uses the S10 Apple Watch chip, several generations ahead of the S5 in the original model.
What makes Siri AI different from the Siri in the original HomePod mini? Siri AI is much more capable now, able to do more than rote tasks like playing a song. Apple says Siri AI has “broad world knowledge,” so it can respond to any questions with answers from the web. It’s also much more conversational.
HomePod mini 2
$149 at Apple							
						
To use Siri AI, the HomePod mini 2 requires pairing with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. It can connect to up to six users in a household and securely access apps such as Messages, Music, Clock, Calendar, Contacts, Mail, and more.
According to Apple, Siri AI on HomePod mini 2 won’t be available immediately, and it is only available in English. So if you pre-order one now, it won’t not have Siri AI right away. When it does arrive, Siri AI is available in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa.
Four-speaker surround sound with new Apple TV 4K

				
					

				
			
Apple




If you decide to get the new Apple TV 4K, you can set up your home theater with four-speaker surround sound using the HomePod mini 2. This setup will identify the speaker locations in the room and properly set the speaker timing and audio level for proper calubration.
Four-speaker surround sound requires matching pairs; you can have four HomePod mini 2s, or matching pairs (front and rear) of the HomePod mini 2s and the 2nd-generation HomePod. It doesn’t appear that the original HomePod mini can be used in this arrangement at all and you can’t mix-and-match stereo pairs.
The HomePod mini 2’s S10 chip analyzes audio in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance, and it still offers 360-degree sound. However, Apple does not specifically claim improved audio quality over the original HomePod mini.
Soundglow
The HomePod mini 2 has a screen with a feature called Soundglow, a “visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble.” Colors that match a song’s album artwork are used, and you can choose a soundscape to create “bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.” However, you’ll need to be standing above or at least near a HomePod mini 2 to see it.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Updated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
The HomePod mini 2 supports Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) and Bluetooth 6, which are upgrades over the 802.11n Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5 in the original HomePod mini. This means that the new device will have faster wireless connectivity and less latency.
The HomePod mini 2 continues to offer Thread connectivity, as well as peer-to-peer discovery. An Ultra Wideband chip is used for device proximity.

				
					

				
			
PInk is a new addition to the HomePod mini 2 lineup.

Apple




New colors
Apple has decided to go with more neutral tones for the HomePod mini 2. It is available in blue, green, pink, midnight, and white. It is no longer available in yellow or orange.
What’s the same
The HomePod mini 2 still have the features of the original HomePod mini, including:
Connectivity with the Mac
Connectivity with smart home devices (Home app and HomeKit)
Stereo audio paring
Four-microphone design for far-field Siri
Multiroom audio with AirPlay
Sound Recognition for smoke and carbon monoxide alarm sounds
Intercom transcriptions
Temperature and humidity sensors
Price and availability
HomePod mini 2 is $149/£149 and is currently available for pre-order now. Shipments begin on October 30.

title: Apple's HomeView Touts These 5 Privacy Features
content:
Apple uses a number of methods to keep HomeView users' personal information private, even when a whole household shares the device.


The device recognizes up to six people, giving each their own Home Screen with personalized apps and widgets. Apple says personal content stays private to each user, while shared photo albums and music can remain available to everyone in the household, including guests.

For content from apps such as Messages and Calendar to appear, HomeView must recognize the enrolled user's face, and their paired iPhone or iPad normally needs to be present and recently unlocked. 

There is an exception when the paired iPhone or iPad disconnects from Wi-Fi. Personal information may remain accessible if the HomeView still recognizes the user and the paired device was recently connected to the same Wi-Fi network, has an active cellular connection, remains in the same location, and has been recently unlocked.

The HomeView's A18 chip includes Secure Exclaves, which is a protected processing environment that handles camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Apple says isolation features across the chip prevent other components from accessing these environments. According to the company, data processed and analyzed within the Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by HomeView's software, apps, users, or Apple itself.

Siri requests have their own privacy protections. The HomeView can handle requests on the device or use Private Cloud Compute, Apple's system for processing requests in the cloud. Apple says data processed through Private Cloud Compute is neither stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else.

title: Apple’s ‘completely personal’ HomeView smart-home hub is built for sharing
content:
Macworld





As widely expected, Apple announced an entirely new product as part of its “Welcome Home” launch experience on Tuesday October 13: a smart-home hub called HomeView.
Described by Apple as “central to the home and personal to everyone in it,” HomeView is available in two versions. Both feature a square 7-inch (1088 x 1088) Liquid Retina touchscreen display, but in one version, this is attached to a domed aluminum speaker base in a design that evokes the classic G4 iMac. This tabletop model’s two elements are connected by a stainless steel hinge, enabling the screen to be tilted to a convenient angle depending on the height of the horizontal surface it’s sitting on. It’s available in four colors: Silver, Space Gray, Rose Pink, and Starlight.
The second version comprises only the screen unit (only in Silver and Space Gray), and is designed to be hung on the wall using three purpose-built mounts. Perhaps surprisingly, this version isn’t cheaper than the model with a base; both cost $299/£299. What’s more, those mounts I mentioned cost extra, ranging from $59.95/£54.95 for the Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector and $79.95/£69.95 for the Power Mount AC Wired to a whopping $129.95/£119.95 for the Power Mount PoE Wired. And if you pick the USB mount you’ll then have to buy a power adapter as well. It’s not a cheap option by any means.
“Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak in the product’s announcement. The idea is that it sits in a shared space and is open to all, but recognises up to six individual users by their faces and adapts its interface and preferences, including the Home Screen, apps, and widgets, to whoever is using it at a given time. Content marked as personal stays private from other users, Apple insists, but other content, such as photos and music, can be shared with other users and guests.

				
					

				
			It’s a lot slimmer without the base, but no cheaper.
Apple




The HomeView runs Siri AI, of course, and consequently gets the benefits of that AI assistant’s much improved capabilities compared to the error-prone version of Siri which ran on the older HomePods. It can answer questions and use natural, conversational language; if paired with a Siri AI-enabled iPhone or iPad, it can surface information from messages, emails, and calendar events. The device can also be used for FaceTime (it supports Center Stage), the Intercom feature known from previous HomePods, and reading out and replying to messages.
Apple talks up HomeView’s entertainment capabilities, pointing for example to the two custom full-range drivers in the display, and the down-firing woofer and two force-cancelling passive radiators in the base, all of which deliver “an exceptional listening experience through a custom-engineered acoustic system.” The speaker elements in the base make it sound like the wall-mounted model will be a weaker audio choice, but Apple assures us that it “delivers rich sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” We look forward to testing all of this out.

				
					

				
			The interface is attuned to your individual needs.
Apple




But what about controlling third-party smart-home accessories? Oddly, Apple doesn’t mention what most of us assumed would be the device’s main function until the 17th paragraph of the press release. But yes: you can control all your (compatible) home tech using the touchscreen or voice commands, and there’s a special Home Modular face for this purpose. If you have a supported iCloud+ subscription and compatible cameras, the device can recognise “people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles” when they appear, and notify the household. And, like the iPhone and more recently the Apple Watch, HomeView can identify the sound of smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and create an alert when it does so.
Pre-orders for both versions of HomeView have already opened for customers in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the U.S., but they won’t hit stores until Friday, November 13.
And there are further issues with availability. While the cheaper two mounts for the wall model can be pre-ordered now, the Power Mount AC Wired won’t become available until “early 2027.” And more seriously, the entire HomeView range is unavailable currently and for the foreseeable future in the European Union, “as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.”

title: Europe's clashing with Apple means no HomeView for the EU
content:
Apple already denies European users Siri AI because of regulatory disputes, but now for the first time its hardware is being affected with no EU release for the HomeView.


HomeView is a hardware Siri AI device, and Siri AI is not available in the EU - image credit: Apple.
The short version is that the European Union's Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires Apple to provide rivals with full access to its technology from day one. Apple argues that no other firm has this burden, and moreover that it dramatically compromises users' privacy.
This is why users in the EU have not had features ranging from iPhone Mirroring and Mac Live Activities, to Siri AI. And it's now why they will not get the new HomeView, at least not at first, and possibly not ever.

title: HomePod mini 2: Everything you need to know release date, price & specs
content:
Macworld





Apple has unveiled the HomePod mini 2, the first major update to its smallest smart speaker since the original launched in November 2020. Announced on October 13, 2026, the new HomePod mini brings Apple’s more capable Siri AI assistant, upgraded audio experiences, improved connectivity, and a selection of new colors. It retains the familiar compact, spherical design but features significantly improved technology inside.
The biggest upgrade is Siri AI, which will bring more natural conversations, broader knowledge, and greater awareness of personal information stored on connected Apple devices. This will allow users to ask more complex questions, find information in messages and emails, and perform tasks across apps. However, Siri AI won’t be available immediately: Apple says the feature will arrive in a future software update, and some personalized features will require a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.
Apple has also replaced the original HomePod mini’s aging S5 processor with the newer S10 chip, enabling enhanced computational audio. Other major additions include four-speaker surround sound when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, the ability to use HomePod mini as a Mac speaker, and Sound Glow, which turns the illuminated touch surface into a colorful display that responds to music. Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6 bring the speaker’s wireless technology up to date.
The HomePod mini 2 comes in five colors: pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. It costs $149, compared with the previous model’s $129 price following Apple’s June 2026 price increase. Pre-orders opened on October 13, with the new speaker going on sale on Friday, October 30. It’s a substantial upgrade for anyone buying their first HomePod mini, although existing owners may find the strongest reason to upgrade is the new Siri experience.
HomePod mini 2 vs. HomePod mini: The 10 biggest changes


FeatureHomePod mini 2 (2026)HomePod mini (2020)

1. ProcessorApple S10Apple S5
2. SiriSiri AI, arriving laterOriginal Siri features
3. Personal contextCross-app personal context with compatible iPhone/iPadLimited personal requests
4. Home theaterFour-speaker surround sound with Apple TV 4K (4th gen)Stereo pairing
5. Mac audioCan serve as a Mac’s default speaker on supported MacsAirPlay audio
6. Visual effectsNew Sound Glow music animationsIlluminated Siri/touch surface
7. Wi-FiWi-Fi 6EWi-Fi 4 (802.11n)
8. BluetoothBluetooth 6Bluetooth 5.0
9. ColorsMidnight, white, blue, green, pinkMidnight, white, blue, yellow, orange
10. Price$149$99 at launch; $129 most recently

 



The biggest improvements are in software intelligence, audio capabilities, and wireless connectivity rather than the speaker’s physical design. Its fundamental audio hardware remains familiar, including the full-range driver, dual passive radiators, and 360-degree acoustic waveguide. 


HomePod mini 2 release date: When will it go on sale?
Apple announced the HomePod mini 2 on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at its “Welcome Home” product launch. The new speaker is available to pre-order immediately, with the official release date set for Friday, October 30, 2026.
Customers in the U.S. and more than 23 other countries and regions can order the HomePod mini 2 through the Apple online store or Apple Store app. It will also be available in Apple retail stores from October 30. Other retailers are expected to stock the speaker, although Apple hasn’t provided a confirmed list of third-party sellers.
The new model arrives almost six years after the original HomePod mini launched in November 2020. Apple had been widely expected to update the speaker in 2025, but reports suggested that development of its redesigned Siri assistant delayed the launch. Although the new hardware is finally arriving, customers will still have to wait for a subsequent software update before they can use Siri AI.
Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.S.
Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.K.


							


HomePod mini 2 design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			The Pink HomePod mini

Apple




Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the HomePod mini for its second generation. The new speaker retains the familiar spherical shape, with a seamless acoustic mesh covering its body and an illuminated touch-sensitive surface on top. It’s designed to fit unobtrusively on a desk, bookshelf, kitchen counter, or bedside table.
The HomePod mini 2 measures 3.3 inches (84.3mm) high and 3.9 inches (97.9mm) wide, exactly the same dimensions as its predecessor. It weighs 335g, making it slightly lighter than the original 345g model. Apple continues to use acoustically transparent fabric, allowing sound to travel through the enclosure in every direction.
The most obvious visual changes are the colors. HomePod mini 2 is available in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. Pink and green replace the outgoing orange and yellow options, while blue has a darker appearance than before. Interestingly, these colors closely match those revealed in Apple software before the announcement, although a previously rumored red version hasn’t appeared.
The other significant visual upgrade is Sound Glow, which makes the illuminated surface on top much more expressive. Rather than simply displaying Siri’s familiar animations, it can pulse and glow in response to the bass and treble of music. Colors can reflect the artwork of the song being played, while soundscapes such as rain produce their own lighting effects.
Apple hasn’t changed the basic touch controls. Users can still tap to play or pause music, double-tap to skip forward, triple-tap to skip backward, touch and hold to activate Siri, and use the illuminated plus and minus controls to adjust volume. The biggest interface improvements therefore come from Sound Glow and the forthcoming Siri AI features rather than new physical buttons.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 processor: What chip does it use?
The HomePod mini 2 is powered by Apple’s S10 chip, replacing the S5 processor used in the original HomePod mini since 2020. That’s a substantial generational leap, bringing the speaker considerably more modern processing hardware and helping to enable Apple’s new AI capabilities and enhanced audio features.
The S10 enables advanced computational audio, allowing the HomePod mini 2 to analyze music in real time and optimize its dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. This processing also supports Apple’s expanded home theater features, including four-speaker surround sound when used with a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
Perhaps more importantly, the new processor forms part of Apple’s push to bring Siri AI to its smart speakers. The redesigned Siri will support more conversational requests, broader world knowledge, and personal context awareness, with processing distributed between the HomePod, connected Apple devices, and Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 connectivity: What’s changed?

				
					

				
			Top of the HomePod mini

Apple




The HomePod mini 2 brings two confirmed wireless upgrades: Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6. These replace the original model’s older Wi-Fi 4 and Bluetooth 5.0 technologies, bringing the speaker up to date with Apple’s latest wireless ecosystem.
Wi-Fi 6E adds access to the 6GHz wireless band when used with a compatible router, potentially reducing congestion and improving network performance in busy homes. Bluetooth 6 introduces newer wireless capabilities, although Apple hasn’t specified which Bluetooth improvements the HomePod mini 2 takes advantage of.
The new HomePod mini also supports Thread networking, allowing it to act as part of a compatible smart-home network. This helps it communicate with devices such as smart lights, sensors, and other supported accessories without relying exclusively on traditional Wi-Fi connections.
Apple lists an Ultra Wideband chip for device proximity, continuing support for proximity-based interactions with compatible devices. However, the technical specifications don’t identify the generation of the chip, so it isn’t yet possible to confirm whether this is an improvement over the original model’s U1 hardware.
Despite earlier rumors about Apple’s in-house wireless networking technology, the company hasn’t named a specific Apple-designed connectivity chip for the HomePod mini 2. The speaker continues to depend on Wi-Fi for its internet connection.


						

							


HomePod mini 2 price: How much does it cost?
The HomePod mini 2 costs $149/£149, making it $20/£20 more expensive than the previous-generation model at its most recent official price. It’s also $50/£50 more expensive than the original HomePod mini was when it launched in November 2020.
Apple initially sold the HomePod mini for $99/£99, but increased the price to $129/£129 in June 2026. The new model therefore represents another price increase, although it brings a significantly newer processor, support for Siri AI, improved connectivity, and additional audio capabilities.
Unlike Apple’s iPhones, iPads, and Macs, the HomePod mini doesn’t come in different storage configurations. There are no higher-capacity versions or additional memory upgrades to choose from, and Apple hasn’t disclosed the storage or RAM included in the new speaker.
Apple hasn’t attributed the higher price to any particular component costs, so it’s unclear whether the S10 chip, memory, new wireless hardware, or other manufacturing expenses influenced the increase. All five colors are available at the same price.


						

							






ModelU.S. priceUK price

HomePod mini (2020 launch)$99£99
HomePod mini (June 2026 price)$129£129
HomePod mini 2 (October 2026)$149£149
Increase over previous price+$20+£20
Increase over launch price+$50+£50

 






Should you buy a HomePod mini 2?
The HomePod mini 2 looks like a worthwhile purchase for anyone looking for an affordable Apple smart speaker, particularly those interested in Siri AI, smart-home control, and multiroom audio. The S10 chip, upgraded connectivity, and new audio features make it a much more capable device than its predecessor.
However, existing HomePod mini owners shouldn’t rush to upgrade. The design and fundamental speaker hardware remain largely unchanged, and Siri AI won’t arrive until a future software update. If you mainly use your HomePod for music, an inexpensive first-generation model could still be a good choice. For more powerful sound, consider the full-size HomePod.

title: Apple HomeView: Everything you need to know about Apple’s smart-home display
content:
Macworld





Apple HomeView is Apple’s first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information.
Powered by Apple’s A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. It can also recognize up to six members of a household, providing a personalized experience while keeping individual information private.
HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple’s existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house.
Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. It comes in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, with prices starting at $299/£299.
What can Apple HomeView do?
HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren’t available on Apple’s traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services.


FeatureWhat’s new compared with HomePod

Smart-home dashboardTouchscreen controls for lights, locks, heating, scenes, and automations
Siri AINatural conversations, broader knowledge, and personalized assistance with a compatible paired device
Personalized Home ScreenRecognizes up to six users by face and provides individual apps, widgets, and content
FaceTime video callsBuilt-in 12MP Center Stage camera for hands-free video calling
Calendar and remindersView appointments, manage tasks, set timers, and access personal information

Music and videoView album artwork, lyrics, videos, and supported streaming content on the built-in display

Messages and communicationRead and respond to messages, make calls, and use Intercom
Recipes and household activitiesFollow step-by-step cooking instructions, manage timers, and access helpful information

 



HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers.
How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad?
The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household.
HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. Its ability to recognize different household members and switch automatically between personalized experiences is particularly useful in a shared space.
However, HomeView isn’t intended to replace an iPad. The iPad remains the better choice for portable computing, productivity, games, and the broad selection of apps available from the App Store. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls.

Announced: October 13, 2026 
Pre-orders: October 13, 2026 
In Store: November 13, 2026
Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its “Welcome home” launch. Pre-orders opened the same day, with both the tabletop and wall-mounted models scheduled to go on sale on Friday, November 13.
HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Singapore pre-orders open on October 15, while customers in South Africa can order through authorized resellers.
The device won’t initially be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t currently available in iOS in the EU. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn’t announced a European release date.
HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. It will also be displayed in Apple Stores. Apple hasn’t announced any general shipping delays beyond the roughly one-month gap between its announcement and retail availability, although individual delivery estimates may vary.
The November 13 date confirms the mid-November launch timeframe reported before the announcement. Earlier speculation about an October 30 launch is now superseded by Apple’s official schedule.
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.S. 
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.K. 


							


Apple HomeView design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			The HomeView

Apple




HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple’s classic iMac G4. A stainless steel hinge allows the screen to tilt, making it easy to adjust the viewing angle when HomeView is positioned on a kitchen counter, desk, or bedside table.
The tabletop model is available in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. The base incorporates the speakers, including a downward-firing woofer, while the display contains two additional full-range drivers. Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable.
The wall-mounted HomeView has a different design, with a slim square enclosure that’s just 0.39 inch thick. It is available in Silver and Space Gray and is designed for locations such as hallways and entrances. Unlike the tabletop model, it doesn’t include a separate woofer and requires a compatible wall mount, sold separately.
Both versions feature a touchscreen, built-in camera, four microphones, and USB-C power. Apple hasn’t listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls.


						

							




HomeView dimensions and weight

 The tabletop dimensions vary depending on the display’s tilt angle.






Does Apple HomeView have a camera?
Yes. Both HomeView models feature a built-in 12-megapixel Center Stage camera with an f/2.4 aperture.
The camera supports FaceTime video calling, with Center Stage automatically adjusting the framing to keep people visible as they move around or when additional participants join the conversation. Four beamforming microphones help pick up voices from across the room while reducing background noise.
The camera also plays an important role in HomeView’s personalized features. It can recognize registered household members by face, automatically switching to their individual Home Screen and making their personal information available when the required security conditions are met.
Apple uses a protected processing environment called Secure Exclaves to isolate facial and voice recognition data from the operating system and apps. The system is designed so that the sensitive camera and microphone information used for recognition isn’t exposed to other users or Apple.
Apple hasn’t published more detailed video recording specifications, such as maximum capture resolution or frame rate.


						

							


What screen does Apple HomeView have?

				
					

				
			
HomeView

Foundry




HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina touchscreen with a resolution of 1088 by 1088 pixels, giving it a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. It uses an LED-backlit IPS panel with Multi-Touch support, True Tone, and a fingerprint-resistant oleophobic coating.
Maximum brightness reaches 500 nits, while minimum brightness drops to just 0.3 nits, making it suitable for a bedside table without lighting up the room at night.
The interface also adapts to proximity, showing simpler information when viewed from across the room and revealing more detail as someone approaches. Customizable faces include Photos, Calendar, Weather, Flow, and Snoopy.
The display is the same on the tabletop and wall-mounted models. Apple hasn’t specified a refresh rate, and there’s no OLED option.


						

							


What processor does Apple HomeView use?
HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, the same generation of processor introduced with the iPhone 16 in 2024. This is considerably more powerful than the Apple Watch-derived processors used in older HomePod models and gives HomeView the processing capabilities needed for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
The A18 is manufactured using a second-generation 3-nanometer process. In its original iPhone implementation, it features a six-core CPU, five-core GPU, and 16-core Neural Engine. Apple hasn’t confirmed whether the HomeView uses exactly the same CPU and GPU configuration, or whether the chip has been adapted for the new device.
The Neural Engine is particularly important because HomeView uses AI to support conversational Siri interactions, recognize household members, process camera and microphone information, and provide personalized responses. Apple’s Secure Exclaves also isolate sensitive recognition data from the operating system and applications.
Apple hasn’t revealed any performance comparisons between HomeView and previous HomePod processors, or disclosed any HomeView-specific improvements to chip packaging or manufacturing. However, the A18’s efficient 3nm architecture should help Apple deliver substantial processing power in a compact device that’s designed to operate continuously.
The A18 was one of the key specifications correctly predicted in our earlier HomeView rumors.


						

							




Apple HomeView connectivity and compatibility
HomeView supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread networking, giving it the wireless connectivity needed to communicate with Apple devices and compatible smart-home accessories.


ConnectivityHomeView specification

Wi-FiWi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO
Wi-Fi bandsSimultaneous dual-band operation
BluetoothBluetooth 6.0
ThreadSupported
MatterCompatible accessories supported
HomeKit / Apple HomeSupported

Ultra WidebandNot listed in Apple’s specifications
Cellular modemNo cellular connectivity announced
Satellite connectivityNot supported or advertised
Wired connectionUSB-C for power

 



HomeView integrates directly with Apple’s Home app and can control compatible smart lights, door locks, thermostats, blinds, and security cameras. It also supports Matter accessories, expanding compatibility beyond devices specifically designed for HomeKit.
Importantly, HomeView can act as a home hub itself. You don’t need to buy a separate HomePod or Apple TV simply to use HomeView as your smart-home hub. However, some advanced features depend on compatible accessories, an iCloud+ subscription, or an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. 
Apple has also announced the Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The first accessories will arrive in December 2026, with additional products following in early 2027.


Which iPhones and iPads work with HomeView?
Apple lists an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later or an iPad running iPadOS 27.2 or later as a system requirement, alongside Wi-Fi internet access.
To use HomeView’s more personalized Siri AI features, you’ll need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Basic Siri AI functions, including general questions and conversational interactions, remain available without an Apple Intelligence-enabled companion device.
HomeView also requires an Apple Account and compatible paired device for each household member who wants access to their personal information.


						

							


Does Apple HomeView have a battery or MagSafe charging?
Neither HomeView model has a built-in battery. Both are designed to remain connected to a power supply, so you can’t pick one up and use it around the house like an iPad.
The standard tabletop model includes a 1.5-meter USB-C cable and a 30W power adapter. Its USB-C connection supplies power rather than functioning as a conventional charging port.
The wall-mounted HomeView also requires continuous power, but Apple doesn’t include the wall mount, USB-C cable, or power adapter. These must be purchased separately, with a minimum 20W power adapter required when using a compatible USB-C power arrangement.
Apple offers three mounting solutions through Schneider Home, including a plug-in USB-C option, an AC-wired installation, and a Power over Ethernet (PoE) version coming in early 2027.


						

							


What software does Apple HomeView use?

				
					

				
			
Like a big Apple Watch

Apple




HomeView runs dedicated home-focused software built around Siri AI, Apple’s Home app, widgets, and a selection of familiar Apple applications. Apple identifies the initial Siri AI software as HomeView software version 27.2.
Rather than providing a conventional iPad interface, HomeView is designed to show useful information at a glance and respond to touch, voice, and proximity. Users can customize their Home Screen with apps and widgets, while special faces display photos, clocks, weather, calendar information, and animated artwork.
What can Siri AI do on HomeView?
Siri AI is one of HomeView’s biggest selling points. Powered by Apple Intelligence, it can answer open-ended questions, understand follow-up requests, draw on broad world knowledge, and support natural conversations.
For example, users can ask Siri to find a recipe, explain something they’re interested in, recommend music, control their smart-home accessories, or help organize everyday tasks.
When HomeView is paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri becomes more personal. It can draw on information from Calendar, Messages, and other apps, helping users locate an invitation, check an appointment, or find relevant information without manually searching their devices.
Siri conversations can also continue across Apple devices using the Siri app, with conversation history privately synced through iCloud.
There are some limitations. Siri AI initially supports English, with Canadian French coming later. Certain AI features that use server-side models have daily usage limits, and Apple says expanded access will eventually be available for a fee. Siri AI launches in beta on HomeView software 27.2.


						

							




Which apps are available on HomeView?
Apple includes a selection of built-in apps and provides access to additional entertainment services through compatible iPhones.


Built-in appsAdditional apps and content

Calendar, Reminders, MessagesApple TV
FaceTime, Find My, IntercomApple News
Music, PodcastsAudiobooks
Home, SafariApple Music Classical
Weather, World ClockCompatible third-party audio and video apps
Alarms, Timers, SettingsSupported content and services from iPhone

 



HomeView supports third-party audio and video apps from compatible iPhones, but Apple hasn’t announced a dedicated HomeView App Store or general installation of iPad apps. That means it shouldn’t be regarded as a replacement for an iPad’s broader software capabilities.


How does HomeView work for different family members?
HomeView can recognize up to six users by their faces, automatically switching between personalized Home Screens and keeping each person’s content separate.
For example, one family member could approach HomeView and see their own calendar and reminders, while another would be shown different information. Shared photo albums, music, and general smart-home controls can still be enjoyed by everyone.
Access to personal information is more tightly controlled. The user’s paired iPhone or iPad must be on the same Wi-Fi network, must have been recently unlocked, and HomeView must recognize the person’s face.
Guests and unrecognized users can still ask Siri questions, play music, check the weather, set timers, and control eligible smart-home accessories, without gaining access to anyone’s private messages or calendars.


						

							


Is Apple HomeView secure?
Apple has designed HomeView with a particular emphasis on privacy, given that it includes an always-available camera and microphones in a shared household space.
The A18 chip uses Secure Exclaves to process camera and microphone data used for recognizing faces and voices. This information is isolated from the operating system and apps, so sensitive recognition data isn’t exposed to other software or Apple.
For Siri requests, HomeView can process information locally or use Private Cloud Compute, which Apple says handles cloud requests without storing the data or making it accessible to Apple.
HomeView also supports HomeKit Secure Video, including intelligent recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles with a compatible iCloud+ subscription. It can provide AI-generated descriptions of recorded activity, although these advanced features require setup with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.


						

							


How much does Apple HomeView cost?
Apple HomeView $299/£299
Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) $299/£299
Apple HomeView starts at $299 in the U.S. and £299 in the U.K., with the tabletop and wall-mounted models carrying the same base price.
This positions HomeView below the $349 full-size HomePod price, although HomeView isn’t necessarily a direct replacement for that audio-focused speaker. 


						

							




Do HomeView wall mounts cost extra?
Yes. While the tabletop HomeView includes the accessories needed for power, the wall-mounted version requires additional purchases.


Schneider Home mounting accessoryU.S. priceAvailability

Power Mount USB-C Wall ConnectorFrom $59.95/£54.95Pre-order now
Power Mount AC WiredFrom $79.95/£69.95Pre-order now
Power Mount PoE Wired$129.95/£119.95Early 2027

 



For U.S. customers, this brings the minimum hardware cost of the wall-mounted HomeView and listed USB-C mount to $358.95, before any additional installation or power accessories.


Should you buy Apple HomeView?
Apple HomeView looks particularly appealing for households already invested in Apple’s ecosystem. It brings together smart-home controls, a capable Siri assistant, video calling, entertainment, and personalized information in a single device that can be shared by everyone at home.
For families, its biggest advantage could be convenience. Being able to see calendars, reminders, weather, timers, and security cameras in a central location, while automatically switching between household members, makes HomeView more useful than a conventional smart speaker.
It’s also attractive for people with extensive HomeKit or Matter smart-home setups. Rather than relying on an iPhone whenever they want to adjust the heating, check a security camera, or activate a scene, users get a dedicated interface that’s always available.
However, HomeView won’t be essential for everyone. If you mainly use Siri to play music, set timers, and control a handful of smart lights, a HomePod mini is a considerably cheaper option. And if you already use an iPad on a stand in the kitchen, you may find that it handles many of the same tasks while offering much greater flexibility.
At $299/£299, HomeView is a premium alternative to smart displays from Amazon and Google. Its strongest selling points are its integration with Apple products, privacy-focused recognition of individual users, and the more powerful Siri AI experience. However, it’s worth remembering that some of those personalized AI features require a recent Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.


						

							


Which HomeView model should you buy?
For most people, the standard tabletop HomeView is the more sensible choice. It costs the same as the wallmounted version but includes a more substantial speaker system, an adjustable display, and the power accessories needed to get started.
The wallmounted version makes more sense if you want a permanent smarthome control panel in a hallway, entrance, or other shared area. Its slim design is more discreet, although the additional cost of mounting accessories and potentially professional installation makes it less affordable.
We’d recommend waiting for independent reviews before deciding whether HomeView’s sound quality, Siri performance, and personalized features justify its price. But for Apple households looking for a central smart-home display, HomeView already offers a combination of features that no existing HomePod can match.

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Everything we know about Apple’s next laptop
content:
Macworld





Apple offers the MacBook Pro with three different chip options. It starts with the entry-level M5 chip, which you can only get in the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple also offers higher end M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro, as it has since the M1 arrived in 2020.
Apple launched the M5 MacBook Pro in October 2025, and the next generation could arrive almost exactly a year later. According to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple plans to announce the entry-level 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, alongside a new iMac, iPad mini, and the first touchscreen MacBook Pro.
The standard M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing design, with the new processor providing the main upgrade. The more substantial changes—including an OLED touchscreen and redesigned chassis—are reportedly reserved for premium MacBook Pro models that will continue to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Apple is reportedly skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation to accelerate development of the M7.
That creates an unusual buying decision: wait for the M6 chip, choose one of the redesigned touchscreen models, or hold out until 2027 for the next generation. Here’s what the latest reports suggest.s.


M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
• October 27, 2026 (reported announcement date)
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple is planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, 2026. According to the report, the launch will include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press.
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to launch alongside the first OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac, and an updated iPad mini. The new entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to retain its 14-inch display and existing design, with the M6 chip providing the main upgrade.
The reported October 27 announcement would fit Apple’s recent release pattern. The M5 MacBook Pro arrived in October 2025, while its predecessor launched in November 2024.
Of the five generations of the entry-level MacBook Pro, three have been released in the October/November timeframe, including the past two releases. Here are the release dates for the entry-level MacBook Pro:
M5 MacBook Pro: October 2025
M4 MacBook Pro: November 2024
M3 MacBook Pro: January 2023
M2 MacBook Pro: June 2022
M1 MacBook Pro: November 2020
Ongoing memory and storage chip shortages could still affect availability or delivery times. These supply constraints have already contributed to price increases across Apple’s Mac lineup. 


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details
12-core CPU and 12-core GPU in the existing M6 Mac mini
TSMC 2nm manufacturing process
Up to 170GB/s memory bandwidth
Improved AI processing with Neural Accelerators

				
					

				
			
The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing.

Apple




Apple has introduced the M6 chip in the Mac mini, giving us a clear idea of what to expect from the upcoming MacBook Pro. The M6 is Apple’s first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm manufacturing process, bringing improvements to CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
The M6 in the Mac mini features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from the M5’s 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It also introduces Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine, boosting performance in AI workloads. The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to benefit from the same architectural improvements, making it particularly appealing to users running AI-powered applications and local AI models.
The Mac mini also provides an indication of what to expect from memory bandwidth. Earlier rumors suggested the M6 could reach 200GB/s, but the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 170GB/s with 24GB or 32GB of unified memory. The 16GB configuration offers 153GB/s, matching the M5. This relatively modest increase could limit the performance gains delivered by the redesigned GPU.
Our analysis suggests that the additional GPU cores, higher clock speeds, and architectural improvements help the M6 deliver gains of 20 percent or more in 3D graphics performance. However, memory bandwidth limitations mean those gains aren’t as substantial as the additional processing power might suggest.
The MacBook Pro’s exact M6 specifications remain unconfirmed, but the Mac mini offers a useful preview of the chip’s capabilities. The key question is whether Apple will make further changes to the processor or memory configurations when it brings the M6 to the MacBook Pro.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features
Existing 14-inch design expected; no OLED or touchscreen
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing 14-inch design, with few changes beyond the processor upgrade. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the display, chassis, and other hardware are likely to remain substantially unchanged from the M5 MacBook Pro.
That means buyers shouldn’t expect an OLED display or touchscreen on the standard M6 model. Those features are reportedly reserved for Apple’s redesigned premium MacBook Pro models, which are also expected to debut on October 27.

				
					

				
			
The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design.

Foundry




How is the M6 MacBook Pro different from the touchscreen MacBook Pro?
Apple is reportedly preparing two very different MacBook Pro updates for October 27.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro will move from the M5 to the M6 processor while retaining its familiar design. It should appeal to buyers who want the newer chip but don’t need a redesigned laptop.
The higher-end MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, are expected to introduce an OLED touchscreen, a thinner and lighter chassis, and potentially an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout. Despite these upgrades, the redesigned models will reportedly use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than M6 Pro and M6 Max processors.
This reflects Apple’s reported decision to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation and focus development resources on the M7 family, which is expected in 2027.
Although the standard M6 is a newer chip, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are designed for more demanding professional workloads, so buyers shouldn’t assume the M6 MacBook Pro will be the more powerful option. It’s a similar situation to the Mac mini lineup, where the standard model features the M6 chip while the higher-end configuration uses the M5 Pro. 
The choice could therefore come down to whether buyers prioritize the latest chip at a lower price or a more powerful MacBook Pro with a redesigned display and chassis.


						

							






FeatureM6 MacBook ProOLED touchscreen MacBook Pro

Expected announcementOctober 27, 2026October 27, 2026
ProcessorM6M5 Pro / M5 Max
Screen sizes14-inchPremium MacBook Pro sizes; expected 14- and 16-inch
DisplayExisting non-OLED displayOLED
TouchscreenNoYes
DesignExisting chassisThinner, lighter redesign
PriceFrom around $1,999Higher pricing expected/

 






M6 MacBook Pro: Price
$1,999/£1,999 starting price possible
We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal.
During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.”
The existing M5 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999/£1,999, following the price increases introduced in June 2026, and the M6 could retain that starting price.
However, another price increase is possible. Ongoing memory and storage shortages continue to affect Apple’s manufacturing costs, and the company may need to pass some of those costs on to buyers.
The redesigned OLED touchscreen models are also expected to carry a premium over the existing MacBook Pro lineup, making the standard M6 a potentially more affordable alternative for buyers who want a new MacBook Pro without paying extra for the redesigned display and chassis.


						

							


Should you wait for the M6 MacBook Pro?
With Apple reportedly planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, there’s a strong argument for waiting before buying a new 14-inch MacBook Pro. The announcement is expected in just a few weeks, and it should provide clarity on performance, pricing, and availability.
Wait for the M6 MacBook Pro if: You’re planning to buy the standard 14-inch MacBook Pro and don’t urgently need a new laptop. The M6 should provide improved CPU, GPU, and AI performance over the M5, without requiring a move to Apple’s more expensive Pro and Max models.
Consider the OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro if: You’re interested in a more substantial upgrade, particularly the rumored touchscreen display, OLED technology, and thinner design. Those models are expected to continue using M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, making them potentially better choices for demanding professional workloads.
Buy an M5 MacBook Pro now if: You need a laptop immediately or find a substantial discount. The existing M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max MacBook Pro models remain capable machines, and a reduced price could make them better value than a newly launched M6 model.
Wait for the M7 MacBook Pro if: You’re particularly interested in OLED but don’t need the touchscreen. Reports suggest Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro could adopt the redesigned OLED chassis in 2027 with an M7 processor, although the timing remains uncertain.
For most people considering the entry-level MacBook Pro, waiting until October 27 makes sense. Even if the M6 doesn’t offer enough of an improvement to justify its price, its arrival could create opportunities to buy the outgoing M5 model at a discount.
