What is it? A premium 3-in-1 Qi2 wireless charging stand with active cooling and a built-in power display.
Who is it best for? iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods owners who want a stylish desktop charger with fast wireless charging and detailed power information.
Who should skip it? Light sleepers, frequent travelers and users who don’t need active cooling or a charging display.
Ugreen’s MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Charging Stand 25W looks different to most wireless charging stands on the market. It’s not a classic charging tree design like the Anker Prime 3-in-1 MagGo Charging Station or Belkin BoostCharge Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand, nor a squat stand, flat pod, or cube.
It closely resembles a modern-day reimagining of the old-style Shure Elvis microphone, with its large silver circular iPhone-charging module ringed with air vents on the sides and a large fan at the rear. It’s not shy of being a statement piece on your desk or nightstand, or frightened to show off its iPhone cooling tech. The iPhone charging module can tilt more than 90 degrees. The Watch module can lie flat or be raised for Nightstand Mode.
How fast does the MagFlow Pro charge each device?
iPhone: up to 25W (iPhone 16 and later); 15W (earlier iPhones)
Apple Watch: 5W
AirPods case: 5W
Those specs mean it should fast-charge each device, although speeds will decrease when all three are used simultaneously—with a maximum output of 32.5W. It ships with its own 45W wall charger so is well covered by that. Although the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 doesn’t include a spare USB-C port itself—look to Mophie’s StealthCharge 4-in-1 Charging Stand for extra ports and cables—you could simply use the Ugreen wall charger for your MacBook, although not as speedily as the iPhone, Watch, or AirPods.
If 25W charging can be sustained, an iPhone could reach 50% in around 30 minutes; 45 minutes at 15W.
An Apple Watch, such as the Series 11, should charge from 0-50% in about 20 minutes.
(We use the 0-50% measurement as batteries charge slower as they get fuller, so the first 50% of a charge is the best comparison when testing different units.)

				
					

				
			The fan at the back of the MagFlow Pro is the largest we’ve seen on any wireless charger.
Simon Jary




How does the MagFlow Pro stay cool?
All that high-powered charging generates heat, especially for the iPhone that can reach 25W for iPhones 16 and later (15W for earlier iPhones).
Most gadgets don’t like hot temperatures that can damage battery life and the iPhone has built-in safeguards that throttle the incoming power if it feels that it’s getting too warm. That means the 25W might be slowed to 15W or less, and even turned off until the phone cools down by itself.
To reduce the threat of the iPhone dialling back the power and therefore the charging speed, Ugreen employs active cooling via the built-in fan. Ugreen calls the 15dB fan “ultra quiet” but you can hear it humming with a rushing wind sound. True, it’s nothing like setting off a hair dryer but it’s definitely audible.
When you’re not in a rush to charge your iPhone, you can turn the cooling fan off with one of the easy-access side buttons (see below). This is certainly recommended if charging by your bedside at night, unless you’re a white-noise enthusiast. Charging overnight doesn’t require the highest speed anyway, so there’s no need for the fan as the iPhone will take in power as it feels fit while you sleep or while you’re working at your desk. But you can turn on the cooling blaster when you’re in a real hurry for power.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




What does the MagFlow’s display show?
There’s a trend for chargers and charging stands to include a real-time display, and the MagFlow Pro’s display is on the front of the arm that suspends the iPhone charger.
The TFT display shows charging wattage for each device, charging surface temperature, and cooling mode. Along the side of the arm are two buttons that you use to switch off the charger and its cooling mode, plus switch from one info-screen to another.
I’m not sure many people other than gadget geeks and tech reviewers—quite the Venn diagram—are going to pay much attention to such in-depth charging data, but it’s handy if you’re a power data control freak.

				
					

				
			The MagFlow Pro’s Apple Watch charging module can lay flat when not in use, and be raised to work in Nightstand Mode.
Simon Jary




What’s it like to use every day?
The MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is an attractive elevated charging stand for a desk or nightstand with tilting iPhone-charging pad, a non-slip AirPods case charging module at the front, and an adjustable Apple Watch charger sat at the back.
It has a small footprint, with a 4.6-inch (117mm) base diameter. It weighs 19.1oz (541g). Charging stands require a decent heft to stay stable. If you want a more portable 3-in-1 travel charger, consider the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Folding Wireless Charging Station, Kuxiu X40 Turbo 25W Wireless Charging Stand, or ESR CryoBoost Foldable 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Station. Ugreen’s own $59 / £43 MagFlow 2-in-1 Foldable Magnetic Wireless Charger is also worth considering but lacks the Watch charger found on the other travel charger.

				
					

				
			iPhone shown in Decoded Silicone Case; Apple Watch with UNIQ Revix IV PANTONE Edition Reversible Apple Watch Band. 
Simon Jary




How much does the Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 cost?
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand is priced at $159.95 / £119.99 direct or on Amazon / Amazon UK.
Check out our reviews of the best wireless charging stations for alternatives, although if you admire this form factor there’s nothing really to stop you ordering one right away.
Should you buy the MagFlow Pro 3-in-1 Charging Stand 25W?
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro is an attractive, well-built charging stand that brings together fast Qi2 wireless charging, adjustable iPhone and Apple Watch charging pads, and a useful display showing real-time power consumption and temperature.
Its standout feature is the built-in cooling fan, designed to help prevent heat from slowing iPhone charging. However, the fan is noticeably audible, which makes the MagFlow Pro better suited to a desk than a quiet bedside table.
At $159.95/£119.99, it’s a premium option, and cheaper 3-in-1 chargers will meet the needs of users who simply want to charge their Apple devices overnight. But if you value its distinctive design, cooling system and detailed charging information, the MagFlow Pro has plenty to offer.

title: How the new Apple Watch sensors affect battery life
content:
Macworld





Apple has radically overhauled the fundamentals of health tracking with the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. They have new sensors that are larger and take readings more frequently. During the day, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure heart rate every five seconds instead of every five minutes. Heart rate variability is also measured more frequently: every five minutes instead of every two hours.
With this increase in frequency, is battery life affected? We tested how this background activity affects the Apple Watch’s battery life. Do you need to worry about battery life, and should you definitely carry a suitable power bank with you?
To find the answers to these questions, I wore an Apple Watch Series 11 on my left wrist and the Apple Watch Series 12 on my right wrist, and analyzed the data from a seven-hour hike. The first half was spent in power-saving mode, the second half in normal workout mode. After the hike, both watches were left running in the background to measure my heart rate, display notifications, and show the time.
The following day, I exported and analyzed the telemetry data from both watches. WatchOS collects telemetry data at 15-minute intervals–in this test, that means that 60 data points were collected for the day (from 8 a.m. to 11 p.m.). A single day does not allow for any general conclusions about battery consumption, but it can indicate a trend.
Whether in power-saving mode or not, an Apple Watch runs continuously in the background during a workout. Both Apple Watches, Series 11 and 12, consistently recorded 900 seconds of background activity per 15 minutes; the power-saving mode setting had no effect on this. What does switch off, however, is the display. On average, it lights up much less frequently in power-saving mode, thereby conserving battery life.
As the energy capacity of each Apple Watch is known in watt-hours and the Battery system setting displays the percentage of maximum capacity, it is possible to calculate how much energy each Apple Watch can consume per hour and per quarter of an hour.
With the new Apple Watch Series 12, which has a 1.461 watt-hour battery and 100 percent of its maximum capacity, 14.61 milliwatt-hours of energy are consumed for every one percent of battery charge. With our Apple Watch Series 11, which has a 1.403 watt-hour battery and 98 percent of its maximum capacity, 13.74 milliwatt-hours are consumed per one percent of the battery charge.

		
			


The overall power consumption chart clearly shows that the two Apple Watches are on a par in power-saving mode. Background activities on both watches are running at full speed, while the display brightness is reduced to a minimum. It is only after power-saving mode is switched off that battery consumption increases on the Apple Watch Series 11. This is because, during that period, it was the actively paired watch and therefore had to deliver notifications and push alerts from the iPhone. The Series 12 was unpaired from the iPhone and did not have to perform these tasks.

		
			


It is also interesting to look at the period after the workout. This is the point that Apple particularly emphasised during the keynote: the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure health data significantly more frequently throughout the day. Between 5:30 p.m. and 11 p.m., the Apple Watch Series 11 recorded 4,222 seconds (70 minutes) of background activity, while the Series 12 recorded 4,883 seconds (81 minutes) of background activity. On average, therefore, the Series 11 is active in the background for 13 minutes per hour, while the Series 12 is active for 15 minutes per hour.
Despite the longer period of background activity, the energy consumption of the two smartwatches differs only slightly. During this period, our Series 11 consumed around 0.248 Wh, while the Series 12 consumed around 0.190 Wh; this difference can be explained by slightly more intensive use of the display on the Apple Watch Series 11.

		
			


Even with the more frequent background monitoring of health data, there is no need to worry about the battery life of the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The system is designed to be energy-efficient, so the more intensive heart rate monitoring does not result in increased energy consumption. You can confidently make the most of the Apple Watch’s new health features and look for power-hungry components in other areas, such as the display.

title: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
content:
Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub.


Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce.

HomeView

Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView, is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM.


Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do:

 
Answer questions with ‌Siri‌ AI

 
Control smart home devices

 
Display the time and weather

 
Display widgets, including widgets from a connected iPhone

 
Show each user their calendar events and reminders

 
Play music, podcasts, and audiobooks

 
Play videos, TV shows, and movies

 
Show photos, slideshows, and home movies

 
Support video calls

 
Show the news

 
Show messages and emails

 
Display recipes and instructions when completing tasks


The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display.

App Store, but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime, Photos, and Mail.

Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room. 

HomePod mini. 

There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray.

Rumors suggest the hub could be priced somewhere around $350.

Apple TV 4K

Apple isn't updating the design of the Apple TV, so expect the new model to be the same boring black box. What's changing is entirely inside.


The ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is going to get a lot more powerful so it can support ‌Siri‌ AI, offering many of the same ‌Siri‌ features that are available on iPhone and iPad in iOS and iPadOS 27.

We're expecting an A19 with 8GB of RAM, along with Apple's N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The A19 will bring a major upgrade in performance, both for ‌Siri‌ and for gaming. It has ray tracing, mesh shading, and other features that will improve gameplay graphics.

gaming controller under the Beats brand, but there's no word on whether it's ready to launch.

Apple will likely emphasize ‌Siri‌ AI and gaming capabilities when introducing the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple raised the price of the current ‌Apple TV‌ to $199 in June, and the new model will be at least that expensive with the processor and RAM upgrades.

HomePod mini

Like the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, the ‌HomePod mini‌ isn't going to get a new design, but it will have internal upgrades that make it more capable. It's going to get an upgraded S10 chip, second-generation UWB for features like Handoff, and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.


You'll need a nearby AI-capable device for ‌Siri‌ AI processing because the HomePod probably won't be able to handle much on-device, but smarter ‌Siri‌ should make for a better experience. ‌Siri‌ AI on ‌HomePod mini‌ will have the context of ‌Siri‌ interactions on other devices, and it's likely conversations will be saved to a connected iPhone's ‌Siri‌ app.

‌Siri‌ AI can answer follow-up questions, handle multi-request queries, and access information from your apps. It'll be similar to having ChatGPT or Claude on a speaker. Though design updates aren't expected, the ‌HomePod mini‌ will get new colors. We're expecting white, blue, black, sage, and pink.

‌HomePod mini‌ pricing went up from $99 to $129 in June 2026, and the new model will likely be priced at $129 too.

LG Accessories

Apple worked with LG to make an LG-branded wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera that will work with the home hub and the ‌HomeKit‌ platform.

The accessories are part of an "Apple Home Collection" that will be marketed alongside the HomeView. They won't be ready until later this year at the earliest, but Apple could show them off during the announcement. 

Announcement Timing

There's no keynote event for the "Welcome Home" product debut, so Apple is probably going to release a video and an accompanying set of press releases. There's an NYC media event that's going to take place at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, October 13, and that could be when all of the announcements happen.

The NYC event will let members of the media get some hands-on time with the new devices to share first impressions.

Pre-Orders and Launch Date

Apple could begin accepting pre-orders just after the new devices launch. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are going to launch on Friday, October 30.

title: Best Antivirus for Mac (2026): Tested & ranked by experts
content:
Macworld





It wasn’t long ago that Macs were considered secure enough on their own. But as Apple devices have grown in popularity, macOS has become an increasingly attractive target for attackers. Today’s threats are less about traditional viruses and more about phishing, fake updates, malicious downloads, and scams designed to trick users into installing malware themselves. Is free antivirus for Mac good enough?
Free antivirus software can provide basic protection, but it often lacks advanced features such as ransomware protection, firewalls and real-time web security. Paid options offer more comprehensive, all-round protection.
Apple includes built-in security tools like XProtect and Gatekeeper, which block known malware and unverified apps. However, in our testing, it was still possible to install Mac malware or suspicious software if warnings were ignored, showing that Apple’s protections alone are not foolproof.
Free third-party antivirus tools offer an advantage in that they are updated more frequently and can protect against a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans and ransomware.
The core antivirus engine is often the same in both free and paid versions. The difference lies in the extra features included in premium suites, such as web and phishing protection, VPNs, identity monitoring, parental controls and customer support.
Ultimately, you get what you pay for. If security is a priority, a paid antivirus offers the most complete protection. However, if you’re on a tight budget, a free antivirus is still better than relying solely on Apple’s built-in security tools.

Importantly, we consider whether these features are genuinely useful or simply added complexity.
Value for money: We evaluate pricing and overall value, including:
Subscription costs and renewal pricing
Number of devices covered
Features included at each tier
Our focus is on products that offer a strong balance of protection, performance and features at a reasonable price.


						

							




Should I get an antivirus for my Mac? 


ScenarioRecommendation

Low-risk user (App Store only, trusted devs, automatic updates on)Apple’s built-in tools are sufficient.
High-risk user (downloads from various sites, torrents, handles sensitive data)Paid antivirus is strongly recommended.
Business user (handles client data, shares files with Windows PCs)Paid antivirus is recommended for an extra safety layer.
User wanting extra features (VPN, password manager, phishing protection)Paid antivirus is worthwhile for the bundled features.

 




 Best Mac Antivirus: FAQ 


1.
Do Macs need antivirus software?
Yes – while Macs are generally more secure than Windows PCs and include built-in protections like XProtect and sandboxing, which helps limit how far malware can spread, these measures are not enough to defend against modern threats such as phishing, adware and ransomware. 
Adding a dedicated antivirus tool helps close those gaps, provides broader coverage against evolving threats and extra layer of security when browsing the web or downloading files.
For more detail, see our guide to whether Macs need antivirus, along with our Mac security tips and advice on how to remove a virus from a Mac.
Do iPhones need antivirus software? 
You may be considering a Mac Antivirus that also offers to protect your iPhone, but is that protection really necessary? 
Apple’s iOS is designed with strong built-in security, including app sandboxing, strict App Store review processes and system-level protections that prevent traditional viruses from infecting your device. This makes it very difficult for malware to spread in the same way it can on other platforms. So, no – iPhones generally don’t need antivirus software.
However, iPhones are not completely risk-free. Threats like phishing attacks, malicious websites and data breaches can still affect users. Instead of installing an antivirus app the best advice is to keep iOS up to date, avoid clicking on suspicious links, use strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and don’t download anything unless you are sure it is safe. 





2.
How does antivirus software protect your Mac?
Mac antivirus software protects your device using a combination of on-demand scans and real-time (always-on) protection.
On-demand scanning checks files when you run a manual or scheduled scan. This can take time, especially on systems with lots of data, and may temporarily use more system resources. For best results, scans are often scheduled to run at convenient times. See how to scan a Mac for malware
Real-time protection works continuously in the background. If malware arrives – for example via an email attachment or downloaded file – the antivirus can detect and block it immediately. Suspicious files are typically quarantined, meaning they are moved to a secure location where they can’t cause harm while you decide whether to delete or restore them.
The effectiveness of these two layers of protection is the most important factor when choosing antivirus software, but additional features can also make a difference.
Many Mac antivirus tools now include ransomware protection, which prevents unauthorised apps from accessing sensitive folders such as Documents or Photos. Only trusted apps are allowed access, and you can customise these permissions.
Web protection is another key feature, often delivered via browser extensions. This helps block malicious websites, phishing attempts and unsafe downloads, reducing the risk of accidentally exposing personal information.





3.
Should my Mac antivirus include a VPN?
Yes, a VPN can be a useful addition to Mac antivirus software. It encrypts your internet connection, helping protect your data – especially on public Wi-Fi. However, built-in VPNs are often limited, so a dedicated VPN service usually offers better performance and features.
Some Mac antivirus packages include a built-in VPN (virtual private network), although VPNs are also widely available as standalone products. For many users, VPNs are appealing because they can mask your location and allow access to region-restricted content, such as streaming services.
More importantly, a VPN improves security by encrypting your internet connection, which is particularly useful when using public Wi-Fi networks. This helps protect your data from interception and reduces the risk of cyberattacks.
While we generally recommend a dedicated Mac VPN service for the best performance and features, a VPN included with antivirus software can still be a useful extra. Just be aware that bundled VPNs often come with limitations, such as data caps or reduced functionality, and may prompt you to upgrade to a full subscription.





4.
What is the best value Mac antivirus?
Value means different things to different users. For some, it’s the best free option; for others, it’s a reasonably priced product with the most useful features. We define value as the best overall balance of protection, performance and features – and for protecting a single Mac, we believe Intego offers the best value.
That said, there are ways to save money on even the top antivirus products. Most Mac antivirus apps are sold as annual subscriptions, often with significant discounts for the first year. When that period ends, you can switch providers to take advantage of new introductory offers, or opt for longer-term plans (such as two- or three-year subscriptions) to reduce the overall cost.
Many antivirus suites also cover multiple devices, including Windows PCs and Android smartphones. If you have several devices in your household, a multi-device plan can offer excellent value. 
For the latest offers, see our guide to the Best Mac Antivirus deals, which includes the most affordable options.





5.
How to spot fake Mac antivirus software?
Because many of us are waking up to the idea that malware is a threat to the Mac, malware writers have made it their business to play on that fear. There have been cases of malware writers disguising their viruses as antivirus apps – two notable examples are Mac Auto Fixer and MacDefender. It’s important to always read reviews on reputable sites such as Macworld before installing any software on your Mac or MacBook.
At the same time, don’t believe everything you read. MacKeeper is a great example of an antivirus program that has got a bad rap, but it’s worked hard to repair its reputation. It has gained Apple Notarization, which means the software has been checked by Apple for malicious components, and the company has garnering certification from various bodies to prove it isn’t a PUP (potentially unwanted program), including an AV-Test certificate. That said, we haven’t recommended it here, and that’s simply because we feel that there are better options available. If you have already installed MacKeeper and wish to try one of our alternative recommendations, we explain How to uninstall MacKeeper.





6.
What can’t Mac antivirus protect you from?
Using a Mac antivirus product, especially one that includes tools to improve your online privacy, may lull you into believing you’re completely safe from personal and private information leaking out and that you no longer need to keep your wits about you. That’s not quite the case. While there’s no reason to panic, you should still practice caution – and there are a few more issues you should consider when using Mac antivirus, too.
First, an antivirus for Mac product may upload the complete text of files flagged to the cloud, where it can be analyzed by separate tools hosted there. This practice is normal and sensible: some malware can detect when a running process may examine it, and will then engage in subterfuge. Antivirus software makers also can access their massive databases to examine files with characteristics that trigger their algorithms – certain elements that match known malware. As a result, security researchers discover new viruses, worms, Trojans horses, and the like. However, helping the greater good means you’ll have to be comfortable with trusting a third-party with your file contents. Where appropriate, we noted privacy policy issues in individual reviews.
Second, this software may also rely partly or entirely on cloud-based checks of URLs, malware, and the like. Accordingly, an antivirus package might upload every URL you visit, metadata about files, signatures of files, information about your computer’s hardware, a list of running or installed applications, and more. Companies vary on their disclosure of such policies, and may not let you opt out of this kind of sharing. We note issues in each review as appropriate.
Third, antivirus software makers also get a sense of what behavior is happening on your computer that’s being monitored or blocked, and may use that information for their own purposes. In some cases, you can opt out of this information gathering.





7.
What virus cleaner does Apple recommend?
Apple has never recommended a third-party virus cleaner, and has instead focused on the Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions found within macOS, which are regularly updated with operating system updates.





8.
How good is Apple’s virus protection?
It’s actually very good, and there isn’t much that gets past it in the way of viruses and malware, given its Xprotect and Gatekeeper features – but these can be overridden, and questionable software can be installed and activated if the user knows what they’re doing.
Still, the protection is present, it’s updated well, and Apple keeps a good eye on things, but new viruses and malware are sent out from bad actors all the time, and this is where a good third-party application can come in handy.
We have tested Apple’s own solution against a range of malware samples. While it did a reasonable job overall, we found instances where questionable applications could be installed without any warning. A helpful analogy is to think of Apple’s built-in antivirus system, XProtect, as the lock on your Mac’s front door, while a paid antivirus solution acts more like an alarm system with security cameras. Third-party tools update their virus definitions – including not just viruses, but also adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware – several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s protections, providing real-time defense against new and emerging threats.
During our testing of Apple’s malware protections, recovery options were limited. In some cases, the only solution was to wipe the Mac and restore from a backup made before the risky behavior – hoping nothing had already spread. Apple does not offer dedicated malware removal support or guarantees if an infection occurs, nor does it protect against cross-platform threats across multiple devices. Paid antivirus software typically includes these services, along with additional features such as web and phishing protection, vulnerability patching tools, VPNs, password managers, parental controls, secure cloud backup, and dark web monitoring.
That said, macOS’s built-in security may be sufficient for low-risk users who install apps only from the App Store or trusted developers, keep automatic updates enabled, avoid pirated software, do not disable Gatekeeper, have limited exposure to risky email attachments, and do not handle sensitive client data.
Ultimately, investing in a reputable security suite for Mac adds an extra layer of protection – and for many users, it’s a case of being safe rather than sorry.





9.
Is there free virus protection for Mac?
The Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions serve as free virus protection for macOS, but you can also get basic virus protection from many of the well-known antivirus providers, we have some recommendations above. 





10.
How to choose the best Mac antivirus for your needs
There are a lot of Mac antivirus programs to choose from. What you want is one that offers a familiar and easy-to-use interface that works well on a Mac – a key reason why we recommend Intego’s antivirus. You should also look for antivirus with a good detection rate – not just for Mac viruses, but also for PC viruses, unless you want to be passing viruses on to friends and clients running Windows. Low impact on system resources is also critical, especially if your Mac isn’t the most powerful model.
Consider the type and number of devices you want to protect – are you looking for an app to cover one Mac, or Mac, iPhone, iPad and even a PC? Your budget matters here, too: do you prefer a subscription model or a one-time payment?
Mac antivirus vendors typically offer different add-ons, and it is certainly a case of you get what you pay for: free products will have fewer bells and whistles, but the most comprehensive Mac security suites will include password managers, parental controls, cloud storage and more. The underlying antimalware engine will usually be the same for all security products from a particular company, so you can save money if you don’t need all those extra features.





11.
When are Apple’s built-in protections sufficient
For many users, Apple’s layered security – XProtect, Gatekeeper and Rapid Security Responses – is more than adequate. If you fit into the “low-risk” category described below, you can probably rely on macOS alone.
You only download apps from the Mac App Store or trusted developers. Gatekeeper ensures that only notarized software from identified developers can run, and XProtect scans these apps for known malware on launch.
You keep automatic updates enabled. Apple regularly updates XProtect’s malware definitions in the background, and with macOS Tahoe, Background Security Improvements can now install critical patches silently without requiring a restart.
You avoid pirated software, torrents, and “cracks.” These are common vectors for malware that can bypass Apple’s checks if a user overrides warnings. 
You do not handle sensitive client data or work in a high-risk environment. For casual home use, the built-in tools are generally enough to block the most obvious threats





12.
When paid Antivirus is worthwhile
Despite Apple’s strong foundation, there are clear gaps that third-party software fills.
You frequently install software from various internet sources. In our hands-on testing, we have found that it is still possible to install malware by ignoring or bypassing Gatekeeper warnings. Our testers were able to install trojans, fake apps, and software that requested access to the microphone, webcam, and keystrokes.
You want protection against phishing and malicious websites. Apple’s XProtect primarily focuses on known malware files. It does not offer the same level of real-time web and phishing protection that suites like Avast One or Bitdefender provide.
You need more frequent updates and broader threat coverage. Third-party tools update their virus definitions several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s updates. They also cover a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware.
You want features like a firewall, VPN, password manager, or identity monitoring. Apple does not offer a dedicated, configurable firewall for macOS (it relies on the built-in one) and does not include a VPN, password manager, or dark web monitoring in its security suite. Paid suites bundle these features.
You share files with Windows users. An unprotected Mac can unknowingly harbor Windows viruses that won’t affect macOS but can be passed on to friends and colleagues. A good antivirus will detect and clean cross-platform threats.

title: You Can Now Set Up Your iPhone Duo Pre-Order - Do It Before Friday
content:
Apple has opened its "Get Ready" service for iPhone Duo pre-orders, allowing customers to pre-select a variety of options to streamline the process of ordering and have a better chance of grabbing one on launch day.


The iPhone Duo launches on October 23, while pre-orders go live on October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time or 8 a.m. Eastern Time. Rather than turn up on the day, however, Apple encourages customers to take action before then and increase the chances of securing their preferred model on day one of sales.

Apple's online store and in its Apple Store app, and it lets you select a preferred color and capacity ahead of time. It also lets you confirm your carrier status, choose your accessories, pick an AppleCare+ plan, select a trade-in, add a payment method, and set a shipping and billing address.

Get Ready is really helpful because when pre-orders go live, it allows you to essentially perform a one-tap order. That's a real advantage when it comes to iPhone Duo, given that supplies are expected to be limited. 

It's been said before about other iPhones, but pre-orders of the iPhone Duo really could sell out within minutes – there have been multiple reports of production issues leading to supply constraints, and users who have completed Get Ready will be able to submit orders faster.

title: Avira Prime for Mac review: Strong malware protection and useful cleanup tools
content:
Macworld





At a Glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Strong core malware protection
Excellent scanning and scheduling interface
Effective junk and application removal

Cons

Inconvenient cookie searching and scan logs
Our Verdict 
Avira Prime offers strong Mac malware protection, excellent scanning and scheduling, and useful cleanup tools. However, its VPN lacks advanced features, Identity Assistant failed during testing, and some malware components were left behind. Despite these shortcomings, it’s a capable security suite worth trying during its 30-day trial.

What is it: Avira Prime is a comprehensive Mac security suite combining antivirus and malware protection with a VPN, password manager, privacy features, and useful cleanup and system-maintenance tools.
Who is it best for: Mac users looking for a comprehensive security suite that combines antivirus protection with useful cleanup, application-removal, and system-maintenance tools.
Who should skip it: Users who need advanced VPN capabilities, detailed security reporting, or dependable identity-monitoring features may find that Avira Prime doesn’t go far enough.
At a glance
Protection: ★★★★☆
Performance: ★★★★☆
Features: ★★★★☆
Ease of use: ★★★★☆
Value: ★★★★☆
There are times when the focus seems right, the execution doesn’t quite match, but there’s still a good utility to be had anyway. Enter Avira Prime, the security and utility suite from longtime developer Avira, which now stands at version 2.3.10 and has been dubbed “Avira Security” at the application level.
Available for macOS 10.15 (Catalina) or later, the latest version combines antivirus and malware protection with a VPN, password manager, privacy features, and a range of cleanup tools. Testing on a MacBook Pro running macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 revealed strong core protection, an impressive scanning interface, and some genuinely useful utilities, alongside a few missed opportunities and one feature that failed to work properly.
Features: What do you actually get?
Avira Prime breaks down into Security, Privacy, and Performance categories from the home screen. The Security category offers Virus Scans, Protection Options, and Quarantine, while the Privacy and Performance sections offer VPN, Passwords, Cookie Cleaner, Identity Assistant, Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, and Startup Apps tools. Other features include a Status indicator, Activity history, and a Scheduler.
There’s a good set of genuinely focused tools here without going overboard, although their usefulness varies.
Malware protection

				
					

				
			Avira Prime’s Full Scan shows the files being checked, elapsed time, and estimated time remaining, making it easier to follow a lengthy malware scan.

Foundry




Antivirus and malware removal remain Avira’s bread and butter, and what’s there is impressive.
The application offers Quick, Full, and Custom Scans, with the latter allowing you to drag and drop volumes for scanning or locate specific volumes, folders, or files through the Finder. It’s a flexible approach that makes it easy to check an external drive or investigate something suspicious without having to run a complete system scan.
This combines with customizable settings for Real-time Protection, Download Protection, and USB Protection, the latter checking USB devices as they’re connected. Avira also integrates well with macOS’s built-in XProtect and Gatekeeper protection features.
The Quarantine tool displays the file paths where malware was discovered, allowing you to review the findings. Unfortunately, the lack of a convenient scan-log export function makes more detailed reporting tedious, particularly if you’re considering Avira Prime as an office systems-administration tool.
VPN and password management
Avira Prime offers VPN functionality through its Avira Phantom VPN application, and the results are something of a mixed bag.
The VPN itself performs well, offering good throughput speeds, reliable streaming, and an easy way to change geolocations as needed. The interface is straightforward, and the core functions should be enough for casual browsing and streaming.
That said, it’s a bare-bones client compared with more advanced VPN applications. Features such as port forwarding and split tunneling are limited or unavailable, and performance through peer-to-peer applications can be substantially slower. What’s present works, but users who depend on these capabilities may want to look elsewhere.
Unlimited VPN data is part of the Prime package, alongside password management and additional privacy tools, while the separate Phantom VPN application also offers a limited free allowance of 500MB per month, along with standalone subscription options. 
Like a number of its competitors, Avira is also chasing the password-management market. The Avira Password Manager extension supports Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Opera, and has you create an Avira account and a master vault password.
Once installed, it was easy enough to create a CSV file from my existing system passwords, which imported cleanly into the extension. From there, the manager activated as needed throughout my normal workday. It’s a useful addition, although anyone already committed to a separate password manager may not find much reason to switch.
Cookie Cleaner and Identity Assistant

				
					

				
			
The Cookie Cleaner lets users select cookies for removal, although the lack of a search function makes navigating large lists harder than it should be.

Foundry




The Cookie Cleaner is an interesting addition and offers tight control over cookie files, but comes with some drawbacks.
Once you’ve activated the feature and quit your open web browsers, the tool quickly scans your Mac’s cookie files. After a few minutes, it presents the dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of cookies that may be present.
The user interface is inviting, but it offers no search function for finding specific cookies, leaving you to scroll through websites and domain names displayed in a scattered, non-alphabetical order. What should be a straightforward process begins to feel like a chore, and a better way of navigating the results is needed.
Avira’s efforts towards an Identity Assistant and overall identity protection are nothing new in the current marketplace, and the feature feels more like an additional value-add than something genuinely unique.
The feature offers dark-web monitoring and allows users to provide personal information they want to track. However, it requires an additional subscription for certain levels of coverage, and the lack of a free trial for these services makes it difficult to judge their value before committing.
More importantly, the feature failed to work properly during testing. Attempts to load the initial scan and personal-information entry screen produced web-based error messages in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Opera rather than a functioning interface.
That server-side error persisted throughout testing, making the Identity Assistant’s actual effectiveness impossible to gauge. It’s disappointing to encounter such a basic problem in a paid security suite.
Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, and Startup Apps

				
					

				
			
Avira Prime’s Uninstaller removes an older version of Blender and its associated support files.

Foundry




Where Avira Prime’s Identity Assistant proved a stumbling block, its Junk Cleaner helped redeem the suite.
As seems to be the convention these days, the feature hunts down cache files, downloads, reports, logs, and Xcode files. On the test MacBook Pro, it offered to clean about 2.67GB of data without automatically going after everything in the Downloads folder, which would have cleared another 46.34GB.
This is backed by an elegant interface that lets you click on specific files and choose exactly which items you want to remove, rather than inadvertently targeting a large swath of data that may be unrecoverable afterwards. It’s a welcome level of control.
Avira’s Uninstaller and Startup Apps features may not be revolutionary, but they’re genuinely impressive in their simplicity.
The Uninstaller allows you to drag and drop an application onto the tool or scan your installed applications, then cleanly removes the selected software and its associated support files. It’s especially useful when you want to remove more than just the main application from the Applications folder.
The Startup Apps tool offers much the same level of control as the corresponding settings in macOS, allowing you to toggle startup items on or off. It’s a convenient addition, although it doesn’t go much further than the tools already built into the operating system.
Test results: How well does Avira Prime protect your Mac

				
					

				
			
Virus scan settings allow users to customize Avira Prime’s protection behaviour and scanning preferences.

Foundry




Antivirus and malware removal remain the strongest parts of Avira Prime, and the new version performed well in hands-on testing against more than 130 malware samples from the Objective-See Mac malware archive.
The application was able to eliminate all but a few of the samples, sometimes deleting chunks of malware as they were extracted from their archives. In these situations, it worked well alongside macOS’s built-in XProtect and Gatekeeper protections, which add their own layers of defence.
Avira Prime wasn’t completely successful, however. Elements of DevilRobber, FlexibleFerret, Lamzev, MacKeeper, notnullOSX, and SentinelSneak remained after testing.
While the software appeared to remove the executable components of some threats, it occasionally left other files behind, including developer-related files. This was worrying, although the presence of leftover files doesn’t necessarily mean that the malware remained capable of executing or causing harm.
These findings are worth bearing in mind. Avira’s core protection is impressive, but it isn’t invincible, and users should not assume that every component associated with a detected threat will necessarily be removed.
The application’s presentation of scan progress is another significant strength. A clear progress bar, elapsed time, filenames, ongoing updates, and an accurate estimated completion time make it easy to see what’s happening. This is one of the better scanning interfaces I’ve encountered in a malware utility in some time.
Independent laboratory results
Avira’s performance is also supported by independent laboratory testing.
In AV-TEST’s June 2026 assessment of Avira Security 2.3 on macOS Tahoe 26.5.1, the software achieved 6 out of 6 for protection, 6 out of 6 for performance, and 6 out of 6 for usability, earning the maximum possible overall result of 18 out of 18.
The laboratory recorded 100 percent detection of the widespread and prevalent malware in its reference set and no false positives in its reported usability tests. 
These results provide a useful independent counterpoint to the occasional leftover malware components observed during our hands-on testing. 
Performance: Will Avira Prime slow down your Mac?
Avira Prime’s scan performance proved solid, particularly when running Quick and Custom Scans.
A Quick Scan completed in just a few minutes, while a Full Scan of more than 633GB of data on the MacBook Pro’s SSD took just under three hours. Given the amount of data being scanned, the latter is the sort of task that might best be scheduled overnight or outside a busy workday.
The Custom Scan option is particularly useful because it allows you to focus on particular files, folders, or volumes rather than committing to a complete system scan every time. USB Protection offers a similarly convenient way to check removable storage as it’s connected.
The June 2026 AV-TEST results also awarded Avira Security 2.3 a maximum score for performance, suggesting that its effects on common activities, such as application launches and file copying, are generally well controlled.
Ease of use: Is it Mac-friendly?
Installation proved as easy as expected, with Avira Prime installing an endpoint security extension and requiring Full Disk Access. The application provided convenient access to macOS’s System Settings to authorize the necessary permissions.
Once configured, the main window offers easy access to the Security, Privacy, and Performance sections. The layout is inviting, with well-organized tools that are straightforward to locate and use.
The settings themselves offer finer control over virus scans, protection options, exclusions or whitelists, and the cookie and junk cleaners.
The Scheduler is particularly good, allowing you to quickly create a roster of recurring Smart Scans and Virus Scans that can be edited later. There’s no need to dig through obscure settings to create a recurring task, and the feature is impressive in its simplicity.
Finally, the Activity section provides a useful reference point for seeing which tests were performed on particular dates, helping complete the picture of your history with Avira Prime.
Not everything is quite as polished. The lack of a search function in the Cookie Cleaner makes navigating large lists unnecessarily difficult, while the limited Quarantine reporting and absence of a convenient scan-log export option become more frustrating when trying to investigate a particular threat.
Overall, though, Avira Prime offers a clean and generally approachable experience that makes its extensive collection of tools relatively easy to manage.

				
					

				
			
The Quarantine tool displays detected files and their locations, although more convenient log-export options would be welcome.

Foundry




Pricing and plans: Is Avira Prime worth the money?
Avira Prime is available as a subscription covering multiple devices across macOS, Windows, iOS, and Android, with introductory pricing that makes the suite more attractive than its longer-term renewal cost.
At the time of testing, the five-device plan was listed at $59.99/£51.99 for the first year, increasing to $109.99/£94.99 annually on renewal. A plan covering up to 25 devices was also listed at $134.99/£116.99 for the first year, with the same figure quoted for subsequent years.
A 30-day free trial is available after creating an account through Avira’s website, with no credit or debit card information required during the sign-up process.
Compared with using Avira Free Security for Mac, the appeal of Prime is therefore largely in the additional utilities and services. The core antivirus features remain strong, but Prime adds cleanup, application-removal, privacy, and VPN capabilities in one subscription.
Whether that’s good value depends on how many of these tools you’ll actually use. The Junk Cleaner and Uninstaller are useful additions, while the VPN is adequate for everyday purposes. The Identity Assistant’s failure to load, however, makes it difficult to recommend paying extra for its additional identity-monitoring coverage.
Avira Prime offers a lot of functionality, but the longer-term cost becomes harder to justify if you only need its antivirus capabilities.
How we tested
Avira Prime 2.3.10 was tested in-house on a MacBook Pro running macOS Tahoe 26.6.2.
Testing included more than 130 malware samples from the Objective-See Mac malware collection, with a focus on malware detection and removal, scanning behaviour, and the application’s ability to manage infected files and volumes.
Quick, Full, and Custom Scans were evaluated, including a Full Scan of more than 633GB of data. The suite’s additional features, including Phantom VPN, Password Manager, Cookie Cleaner, Identity Assistant, Junk Cleaner, Uninstaller, Startup Apps, and Scheduler, were also examined for functionality and ease of use.
Results were compared with independent AV-TEST laboratory findings where applicable.
Should you buy Avira Prime for Mac
The new version of Avira Prime proves to be one of the better antivirus and anti-malware utilities I’ve tested in some time, although there are still areas that need improvement.
Its malware scanning interface, scheduler, junk removal, and application-removal tools are genuinely impressive, and the overall suite offers a useful set of features without becoming excessively complicated.
The occasional malware components left behind during testing are a concern, while the Cookie Cleaner’s lack of search, limited scan-log exports, and the server-side error that made Identity Assistant impossible to evaluate all represent missed opportunities. The bare-bones VPN also won’t suit everyone, particularly users who need more advanced networking features. 
These issues aren’t necessarily deal-breakers, but they’re worth considering alongside the subscription price, especially after the introductory offer expires.
Despite these shortcomings, Avira Prime’s core security and maintenance functions remain strong. It’s well worth evaluating during the advertised 30-day trial to determine whether its combination of protection and additional utilities is right for you.
See how Avira Prime compares to other Mac antivirus solutions in our round up of the best.

title: Should you buy the MacBook Pro now or wait for the M6 or Touchscreen MacBook?
content:
Macworld





If you’re thinking of buying a MacBook Pro, it could be worth waiting a little longer. Apple is reportedly preparing two MacBook Pro updates for October 27, including a new entry-level model with the M6 chip and redesigned higher-end models featuring OLED touchscreens.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro is expected to gain Apple’s new M6 processor while retaining its existing design. The redesigned MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, could introduce thinner and lighter bodies, OLED touchscreens, and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips – becoming Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro.
With new models potentially arriving within weeks, we’d recommend waiting unless you need a MacBook Pro immediately or find a particularly good discount on the current M5 models. Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500 in June 2026, so discounts and refurbished models remain worth considering.
The MacBook Pro is best suited to creative professionals, software developers, engineers and other power users who need sustained performance, a premium display, plenty of ports and high memory configurations. If your workload consists mainly of web browsing, office work, studying or light creative tasks, the MacBook Air is likely to offer better value at a much lower price. In this guide, we’ll explain whether you should buy now or wait, which MacBook Pro is right for you, the best times of year to buy, today’s best deals, and whether a refurbished model or MacBook Air might be a better choice.


Should you buy a MacBook Pro now? 
With new MacBook Pro models reportedly arriving on October 27 2026, we’d recommend waiting before buying. The upcoming M6 model should bring better performance to the entry-level MacBook Pro, while the redesigned M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer significant display and design improvements. However, the existing MacBook Pro lineup remains an excellent choice if you find a substantial discount.
Buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You’re upgrading from an Intel Mac: Apple is ending support for Intel Macs, so if you haven’t yet switched to Apple Silicon, now is a good time to do so. As Intel Macs reach the end of support, they’ll stop receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to newly discovered security flaws.
You need a new laptop: If your current Mac is broken, unreliable or slowing you down, there’s little reason to wait.
You edit video or create content: Whether you’re editing 4K video, working in Photoshop or Lightroom, producing music or creating 3D graphics, the MacBook Pro delivers the sustained performance creative professionals need.
You’re a software developer, engineer or AI professional: Compiling code, running virtual machines, working with AI models or processing large datasets is much faster on the MacBook Pro, particularly the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.
You need sustained performance: Unlike the fanless MacBook Air, the MacBook Pro uses active cooling to maintain peak performance during long exports, renders and other demanding workloads.
You need professional features: The MacBook Pro offers a Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe charging and higher memory and storage options than the MacBook Air.
You find an excellent deal: With new models expected on October 27, retailers may offer bigger discounts on the existing M5 lineup. If you don’t need the latest chip or touchscreen design, a discounted M5 MacBook Pro could be excellent value.


						

							


When shouldn’t you buy a MacBook Pro?
The MacBook Pro is an excellent laptop, but it isn’t the right choice for everyone. If you don’t need its extra performance or professional features, you’ll save money – and probably be just as happy – with a MacBook Air. There are also a few situations where it’s worth waiting rather than buying today.
Don’t buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You already own a recent MacBook Pro: If you have an M2, M3 or M4 MacBook Pro, the performance improvements offered by the M5 generation are relatively modest.
You’re waiting for the redesign: Apple is reportedly preparing OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models with thinner, lighter designs and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for October 27.
You want the next-generation chips: The entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro is expected to gain the M6 chip on October 27, bringing improvements in CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
You’re looking for the best price: With new MacBook Pro models reportedly arriving soon, discounts on the existing M5 generation could become more attractive. Black Friday may bring further savings.
You mainly use your laptop for everyday tasks: If your workload consists of web browsing, Microsoft Office, streaming, email, video calls or light photo editing, a MacBook Air offers excellent performance for much less money.
You’re a student with basic computing needs: If your coursework mainly involves writing essays, researching online or creating presentations, a MacBook Air is likely to be the better value.
Portability is your priority: The MacBook Air is thinner, lighter and completely silent thanks to its fanless design.
You’re on a budget: The MacBook Air delivers outstanding performance for most users while costing significantly less than the MacBook Pro.
For most people, the MacBook Air is the better buy. The MacBook Pro only comes into its own if you regularly run demanding professional workloads that benefit from its active cooling, more powerful chips, superior display, additional ports and higher memory options.

When is the best time to buy a MacBook Pro?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




If you’re looking for the lowest price on a MacBook Pro, the best times to buy are during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day in June/July or October and Black Friday.
Black Friday is typically the strongest shopping period for MacBook Pro deals, although the lowest prices are often reserved for older or clearance models, and popular configurations can sell out quickly.
Another time to look for deals is shortly after Apple launches a new model, as retailers often discount the previous generation to clear remaining stock, making it possible to save hundreds if you don’t need the latest chip.
If you’re a student, you can save all year. Students, teachers, and education staff can typically save $100 to $200 on a new MacBook Pro through Apple’s Education Store. However, the best time to buy is usually during Apple’s annual Back to School promotion in the summer, when qualifying customers can often claim a free pair of AirPods or another bonus gift alongside the education discount. Is buying a refurbished MacBook Pro a good idea?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Buying a refurbished MacBook Pro can be a great way to save money – particularly if you buy directly from Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store.
As of July 2026, buying refurbished makes more sense than ever because Apple has continued to sell refurbished Macs at pre-price-hike prices, allowing buyers to avoid the $300 to $500 increases Apple introduced on new MacBook Pro models in June.
Apple Certified Refurbished Macs are typically around 15% cheaper than brand-new models and come with the same one-year warranty, 90 days of complimentary technical support, and the option to purchase AppleCare+. Every Mac undergoes extensive testing, is cleaned and inspected, and receives genuine Apple replacement parts where necessary.
The main downside is availability. Stock changes daily, so you may need to wait for the exact model, storage capacity, memory configuration, or colour you want. Newer MacBook Pro models also usually don’t appear in the refurbished store until several months after launch.
Third-party retailers, including Amazon, also sell refurbished Macs, but quality standards vary considerably. We generally recommend avoiding Macs that are more than five years old, as they may receive fewer years of macOS and security updates. In some cases, retailers also offer larger discounts on new, previous-generation MacBook Pro models during major sales events, so it’s always worth comparing prices before you buy.
For most buyers, Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store remains the safest and best-value way to buy a refurbished MacBook Pro.

Which MacBook Pro to choose
Before choosing a MacBook Pro, bear in mind that Apple is reportedly preparing new models for October 27. The entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to gain the M6 processor, while the higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max models could receive an OLED touchscreen redesign. Unless you need a laptop immediately, we’d recommend waiting to compare the new models before buying.
Choose the M5 MacBook Pro if you want Pro features such as the better display, extra ports and active cooling, but don’t need the power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max.
Choose the M5 Pro MacBook Pro if you’re a professional who regularly edits 4K video, compiles large software projects, works with RAW photos, produces music or runs multiple demanding applications at once. For most creative professionals and developers, the M5 Pro offers the best balance of performance and price.
Choose the M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work pushes a laptop to its limits. The M5 Max is designed for users editing multiple streams of 8K video, creating complex 3D animations, running large AI or machine learning workloads, or handling visual effects and other GPU-intensive tasks. Unless you regularly perform these types of work, the M5 Pro is likely to offer better value. 


						

							


What about the MacBook Air?

				
					

				
			
The MacBook Air is a good alternative at a lower price.

Stephan Wiesend




If you’re considering a MacBook Pro, it’s also worth looking at the MacBook Air. Apple updated the Air in March 2026, and with a starting price of $1,299/£1,299 (the price increased by $200/£200 in June 2026), it’s significantly cheaper than the MacBook Pro.
The MacBook Air is a good choice if you:
Mainly browse the web, use Microsoft Office or stream media.
Are a student or home user with light computing needs.
Value portability and a silent, fanless design.
Want the best value MacBook.
However, the lower price comes with a few compromises. Compared to the MacBook Pro, the Air offers lower sustained performance, a less advanced display, fewer ports, and lower memory and storage limits.
Choose the MacBook Pro if you need:
Sustained performance for video editing, coding, 3D rendering or AI workloads.
A Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion and HDR.
More connectivity, including HDMI, an SDXC card slot and additional Thunderbolt ports.
Higher-end M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, with up to 128GB of unified memory.
For most everyday users, the MacBook Air is the better value. But if your work regularly pushes your laptop to its limits, the MacBook Pro is well worth the extra investment.


						

							


Do you need to upgrade your current Mac?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Whether you need to upgrade depends on three things: how old your Mac is, whether Apple still supports it, and whether it can keep up with the apps and features you use every day.
If you have an Intel Mac, it’s time to upgrade
With macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has ended support for Intel Macs. While Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for the small number of Intel Macs that support macOS 26 Tahoe, that support is likely to last only another year or two.
The only Intel Macs that can run macOS Tahoe are:
16-inch MacBook Pro (2019)
13-inch MacBook Pro (2020, four Thunderbolt ports)
27-inch iMac (2020)
Mac Pro (2019)
If your Mac isn’t on this list, it may no longer receive the latest macOS updates and will eventually stop receiving security updates. For more advice, read How long Macs and MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.
If you’re still using an Intel Mac, we recommend upgrading as soon as your budget allows. Moving from Intel to Apple Silicon is one of the biggest upgrades Apple has ever offered. You’ll benefit from dramatically faster performance, much longer battery life, quieter operation, Apple Intelligence support, and many more years of macOS compatibility. Read our guides to macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate to see what you’ll gain by upgrading.

Existing first-generation Apple Watch Ultra owners can reasonably keep their watch for another year if its battery still covers their usual days and workouts. Losing support for ‌watchOS 27‌ is significant, but it does not prevent the original Ultra from continuing to handle notifications, activity tracking, navigation, and its other existing features. Owners satisfied with those capabilities may prefer to eke out another year of use and wait to see whether next year's model offers a more substantial upgrade.

However, the Ultra 4 is a worthwhile upgrade for anyone already running into the original model's limitations. The new Health Sensing System provides more detailed heart-rate and recovery insights, while sleep apnea and hypertension notifications expand its health capabilities. These changes are most compelling if you will use the additional information to follow changes in your daily condition or adjust your training.

Longer battery life and satellite connectivity strengthen the case for owners who record extended workouts or regularly travel beyond cellular coverage. If your original Apple Watch Ultra now struggles to finish an outing without charging, the improved battery life is a practical reason to replace it. The larger, brighter display, newer gestures, Audio Intelligence, and expanded Precision Finding support also make the cumulative upgrade more noticeable in everyday use.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are premium true wireless earbuds from Apple. Released in September 2025, they add heart-rate monitoring, foam-infused eartips, stronger ANC, improved sound, longer battery life and IP57 water resistance.
Why we like them
The AirPods Pro 3 refine an already excellent formula with noticeably better comfort, stronger noise cancellation, richer sound and longer battery life while keeping the same launch price. Heart-rate tracking is a useful bonus, making them an easy recommendation for most Apple users.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for iPhone users wanting premium wireless earbuds with excellent noise cancellation, secure all-day comfort and seamless Apple ecosystem integration. They’re especially appealing for fitness enthusiasts who can benefit from the new built-in heart-rate monitoring.
What are the biggest strengths
More comfortable foam-infused eartips with five sizes
Excellent fit that stays secure during exercise
Improved sound with deeper bass and wider soundstage

Longer battery life without a price increase

Few genuinely new audio innovations

Heart-rate tracking only works during workouts
What is battery life like
Battery life increases to around eight hours with ANC enabled, while the case provides roughly 16 additional hours. A five-minute charge delivers about one hour of listening time.
How good is the ANC
Active Noise Cancellation is substantially improved, thanks to new microphones, redesigned eartips and computational enhancements. Apple claims twice the ANC of the previous generation, with noticeably better Transparency mode too.
Verdict
The AirPods Pro 3 aren’t a revolutionary upgrade, but they successfully improve almost every aspect of Apple’s best earbuds. Better fit, stronger noise cancellation, richer sound, longer battery life and useful heart-rate tracking make them easy to recommend. AirPods Pro 2 owners may not need to upgrade immediately, but everyone else gets one of the best premium wireless earbuds available.

The Apple AirPods 5 (with Wireless Charging Case) are open-fit wireless earbuds featuring the H2 chip, improved Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Transparency mode, Conversation Awareness, and Personalized Spatial Audio. The $149/£139 version adds wireless charging, touch-sensitive volume controls, and a Find My speaker in the case.
Why we like them
The AirPods 5 bring better sound and stronger noise cancellation to Apple’s familiar open-ear design, while costing less than the AirPods 4 with ANC they replace. In the review from our sister website, Macwelt, the AirPods 5 were found to deliver a slightly richer, warmer sound than their predecessors and surprisingly effective noise cancellation, making them an excellent alternative to the more expensive AirPods Pro.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for iPhone users who dislike silicone ear tips but still want effective ANC and premium features. They’re particularly well suited to everyday listening, commuting, and anyone who wants many of the AirPods Pro’s features without paying $249. The Wireless Charging Case version is the better choice for most buyers.
What are the biggest strengths
Rich, detailed sound with slightly warmer bass than AirPods 4
Excellent ANC for an open-ear design, particularly against steady background noise
Adaptive Audio and improved Transparency mode
Convenient swipe controls for adjusting volume
Wireless charging via Qi or an Apple Watch charger
Find My speaker built into the charging case
What are the compromises
Open design limits noise isolation compared with AirPods Pro
Fit remains unchanged from AirPods 4 and depends on ear shape
Higher-frequency sounds, including keyboard clicks, remain noticeable
Battery life trails many competing earbuds
No heart-rate monitoring or AirPods Pro hearing-health features
Discounted AirPods Pro 3 can narrow the price gap
What is battery life like
Apple rates the Wireless Charging Case model for up to five hours with ANC enabled, or seven hours with noise control off. The case extends ANC listening time to 22 hours. Macwelt’s testing achieved approximately four hours and 45 minutes indoors, dropping to four hours and 15 minutes when traveling with higher volume settings and Spatial Audio enabled.
How good is the ANC
Noise cancellation is particularly impressive for earbuds that don’t seal the ear canal. Macwelt’s testing found that the AirPods 5 effectively reduced steady background sounds, including road noise and computer fans. Apple claims up to 50 percent better noise cancellation than AirPods 4 with ANC. However, sharper sounds still get through, and the AirPods Pro 3 provide significantly stronger isolation.
What about the cheaper AirPods 5?
Apple also sells the standard AirPods 5 for $129/£119. These include the same H2 chip, sound improvements, and ANC, but have a USB-C-only charging case without wireless charging or a Find My speaker. They also lack the stem-based volume controls and have slightly shorter battery life, offering four hours with ANC and 20 hours with the case. For just $20/£20 more, the Wireless Charging Case model is worth the upgrade, although the cheaper version remains excellent value.
Verdict
The AirPods 5 (with Wireless Charging Case) are among the best open-ear wireless earbuds available. They combine richer sound, impressively effective noise cancellation, useful smart features, and convenient wireless charging at a lower price than their predecessors. Battery life is still fairly modest, and the unchanged fit won’t suit everyone, but they’re an excellent everyday choice for iPhone users who prefer an open design. With the added convenience of volume controls and wireless charging for just $20 more than the standard model, they’re the AirPods 5 we’d recommend.

Why We Like Them
The Momentum True Wireless 5 (TW5) improves on its predecessor in several ways. The sound quality is excellent, with support for the AAC codec for Apple devices and aptX Adaptive/Lossless for Android. This model also gets an update to the latest Bluetooth 6.0, and supports Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. The design is improved too, with smaller earbuds that fit more comfortably, along with an IP54 rating for water and dust-resistance. Even the charging case is improved, with a more compact design, and support for both USB-C and wireless charging.
Who Are They Best For?

The Beats Solo Buds are affordable true wireless earbuds made by Beats, an Apple company. Released in mid-2024, they feature a tiny USB-C charging case, four ear tip sizes and 18-hour battery life.
Why we like them
The Beats Solo Buds deliver impressive value with punchy, enjoyable sound, an exceptionally long battery life for earbuds, and a secure fit thanks to four sizes of silicone ear tips. They’re comfortable, easy to control using physical buttons, and outperform older standard AirPods in several key areas.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for budget-conscious listeners who want reliable everyday wireless earbuds with long battery life and comfortable fit. They’re particularly well suited to Apple users, but also work well with Android devices, making them a versatile affordable option.
What are the biggest strengths
Clear, punchy sound that exceeds expectations for the price.
Outstanding 18-hour battery life from the earbuds.
Secure fit with four sizes of silicone ear tips.
Compact, lightweight case that’s easy to carry.
Physical button controls are simple and reliable.
Excellent value compared with similarly priced rivals.
What are the compromises
No active noise cancellation or transparency mode.
Charging case has no built-in battery for top-ups.
Lacks automatic device switching and multipoint Bluetooth.
No in-ear detection for automatic play/pause.
Call voice isolation isn’t as strong as premium earbuds.
No personalised Spatial Audio features.
What is battery life like
Battery life is excellent. The earbuds are rated for up to 18 hours on a single charge, outperforming many rivals, although the charging case must be plugged into USB-C to recharge them.
How good is the ANC
There isn’t any active noise cancellation. Instead, the silicone ear tips provide passive noise isolation, reducing some outside sound, but they can’t match dedicated ANC earbuds in noisy environments.
Verdict
The Beats Solo Buds prove you don’t need to spend a fortune for enjoyable wireless earbuds. Their clear sound, secure fit and exceptional battery life make them an excellent value buy, especially for everyday listening. While you’ll miss premium features like ANC, multipoint Bluetooth and a battery-equipped charging case, they’re an easy recommendation for budget-conscious shoppers

The Bowers & Wilkins Pi6 are premium true wireless noise-cancelling earbuds from British audio specialist Bowers & Wilkins, featuring 12mm drivers, Bluetooth 5.4, IP54 durability and multipoint connectivity.
Why we like them
The Pi6 deliver the refined, engaging sound quality Bowers & Wilkins is known for at a more accessible price than the flagship Pi8. They’re comfortable for extended listening, offer useful app customisation, solid battery life and excellent overall value despite a few premium feature omissions.
Who are they best for?
They’re ideal for listeners who prioritise sound quality over cutting-edge features. Frequent commuters, music lovers and anyone wanting premium wireless earbuds around AirPods Pro pricing will appreciate their balanced audio, comfortable fit and dependable battery performance.
What are the biggest strengths?

What are the compromises?
